# Staggered-Adoption DiD: How the New Estimators Differ, Which One Dominates Applied Practice, and What They Do (and Don't) Fix About Pre-Trend Testing

## Direct Answer

All three post-Goodman-Bacon estimator families — Callaway and Sant'Anna's (2021) two-stage group-time aggregation, Sun and Abraham's (2021) interaction-weighted estimator, and Borusyak, Jaravel and Spiess's (2024) imputation estimator — solve the same problem the same way at the conceptual level: they decompose staggered DiD into "clean" comparisons that never use already-treated units as controls, then aggregate with transparent, researcher-chosen weights. None requires treatment-effect homogeneity. They diverge on four practical axes: (1) **comparison group** (never-treated vs. not-yet-treated vs. last-treated vs. all untreated observations pooled); (2) **base period** (CS uses only the last pre-treatment period g−1 per cohort; BJS pools all pre-treatment periods via a TWFE outcome model fit on untreated observations); (3) **parallel-trends scope** (CS uniquely allows PT conditional on covariates with doubly robust estimation; SA and BJS require unconditional PT); and (4) **efficiency** (BJS is semiparametrically efficient under unrestricted heterogeneity, delivering confidence intervals roughly 50% shorter than CS and 2–3.5× shorter than SA in simulations and applications — but only because it leans hardest on a correctly specified untreated-outcome model across the whole panel).

On dominance: **Callaway–Sant'Anna is the modal default heterogeneity-robust estimator in applied labor and health economics for 2020–2024**, triangulated from citation intensity (~10,750 citations in six years per Cunningham's package audit; six independent software implementations), synthesis-paper emphasis (CS receives 21 mentions across 4 sections of Roth, Sant'Anna, Bilinski and Poe's *Journal of Econometrics* 2023 review vs. 11 for Sun–Abraham, 7 for de Chaisemartin–D'Haultfœuille, 5 for BJS), and software ecosystem maturity. But "dominance" is real only in *direction*, not *exclusivity*: the operative applied norm became "report a heterogeneity-robust estimator (usually CS) plus a Sun–Abraham event study and/or an imputation robustness check," and no systematic bibliometric audit of AER/QJE/JPE labor and health papers exists — a gap I flag explicitly below. BJS adoption lagged in the published 2020–2024 window because the *Review of Economic Studies* version appeared only in late 2024, though its working-paper incarnation was already influential.

On justification: applied authors in top journals **rarely run their own Monte Carlo simulations** to choose among estimators. Justification typically consists of citing the critique literature, reporting multiple estimators side by side (institutionalized by wrapper packages like `did2s` and `event_study` that run all modern estimators under one syntax), and — increasingly after 2023 — appending Rambachan–Roth "HonestDiD" sensitivity bounds. The Monte Carlo evidence is supplied by the methods papers themselves and by a handful of field replication studies.

On Roth (2022): the new estimators address the pre-trend critique only partially and indirectly. Sun–Abraham eliminates *spurious* pre-trends caused by heterogeneity contamination; BJS separates estimation from testing architecturally (a result qualified by a spherical-errors assumption); CS provides a joint pre-test with simultaneous inference that plugs into power diagnostics. The low-power and pre-test-bias problems Roth documented are genuinely answered only by the complementary layer — power/equivalence diagnostics (Roth's `pretrends` package) and Rambachan–Roth sensitivity analysis — not by the heterogeneity-robust estimators alone.

---

## 1. The Critique and Its Quantitative Baseline

**Goodman-Bacon (2021), "Difference-in-Differences with Variation in Treatment Timing," *Journal of Econometrics* 225(2): 254–277** ([DOI](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0304407621001445); [NBER WP w25018](https://www.nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w25018/w25018.pdf)). The decomposition theorem shows the two-way fixed effects (TWFE) DiD coefficient equals a weighted average of *all possible* 2×2 group/time DiD estimators in the data. Three consequences drive the crisis:

1. **Forbidden comparisons.** Some component 2×2s compare units treated at different times, using the later-treated group as a control before its treatment begins *and* the earlier-treated group as a control after its treatment begins. Once the earlier cohort's effects arrive, using it as a control subtracts its own treatment dynamics from the contrast.
2. **Variance-driven, economically arbitrary weights.** Weights are proportional to timing-group sizes and to the variance of the treatment dummy in each pair — maximized at p(1−p) = 0.25 for units treated in the *middle* of the panel and vanishing for units treated at the panel edges.
3. **A dual identifying requirement.** Causal interpretation of TWFE requires *both* parallel trends *and* treatment effects constant over time. Negative weights arise precisely when average effects vary over time — so the TWFE coefficient can be negative even when every cohort-time ATT is positive.

**Parallel negative results.** De Chaisemartin and D'Haultfœuille (2020, *AER* 110(9): 2964–2996; [link](https://www.aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257/aer.20181169)) independently showed TWFE identifies a weighted sum of group-period ATEs "with weights that may be negative," so the coefficient "may for instance be negative while all the ATEs are positive"; in the applications they revisited, roughly half the weights were negative and one application's sign flipped under their alternative estimator. Sun and Abraham (2021) added the dynamic dimension: in event-study TWFE, the coefficient on a given lead or lag is contaminated by effects from *other* relative periods, and "apparent pretrends can arise solely from treatment effects heterogeneity" — the result that links the staggered-adoption critique directly to the pre-trend-testing debate. Athey and Imbens (*JoE* 2022; [link](https://ideas.repec.org/a/eee/econom/v226y2022i1p62-79.html)) supplied the design-based caveat: under *randomly assigned* adoption dates, standard DiD is unbiased for a particular weighted average causal effect — but timing is rarely random in practice.

**Scale of exposure.** De Chaisemartin and D'Haultfœuille's survey ([NBER WP w29691](https://www.nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w29691/w29691.pdf); published *Econometrics Journal* 2023) reports that **26 of the 100 most-cited AER papers from 2015–2019 estimate at least one TWFE regression**, and that 20% of all empirical AER articles in 2010–2012 did so. Baker, Larcker and Wang (2022, *JFE* 144(2): 370–395; [link](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0304405X22000204)) counted 751 DiD papers in top finance and accounting journals (2000–2019), of which roughly half (~49%; 50% in finance, 47% in accounting) used staggered designs, with ~97% of the staggered papers published since 2010 — and found that re-examining published results with the alternative estimators "differ[ed] substantially from prior papers." Currie, Kleven and Zwiers (2020) document that almost 25% of NBER applied-micro working papers reference DiD; Goldsmith-Pinkham's updated credibility-revolution audit ([NBER WP w35051](https://www.nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w35051/w35051.pdf)) finds 63% of applied-micro papers mention experimental or quasi-experimental methods as of 2024, with growth driven overwhelmingly by DiD. One widely circulated replication exercise (a recent preprint of weaker provenance) reports TWFE and Callaway–Sant'Anna point estimates differing by more than 20% in 38% of 200 replicated staggered studies, with sign disagreements in 7% and bias correlating r = 0.72 with cohort heterogeneity — directionally consistent with the better-documented audits, though I would not lean on those precise figures.

---

## 2. How the Three Solutions Handle Heterogeneity and Dynamic Timing

### 2.1 Callaway–Sant'Anna (2021): Two-Stage Group-Time Aggregation

[*JoE* 225(2): 200–230](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0304407620303948); [paper PDF](https://psantanna.com/files/Callaway_SantAnna_2020.pdf); [package docs](https://bcallaway11.github.io/did/articles/did-basics.html).

**Estimand first.** CS define the group-time average treatment effect ATT(g,t) = E[Y_t(g) − Y_t(0) | G_g = 1] — the average effect at calendar time t for the cohort first treated at g. Heterogeneity is not a nuisance; it *is* the object. Stage 1 identifies each ATT(g,t) from a long difference relative to the cohort's last pre-treatment period (base period g−1) against a clean comparison group. Stage 2 aggregates with researcher-chosen weights along four margins: overall ATT, cohort-specific, calendar-time, and event-study (by length of exposure e = t − g).

**Comparison-group choice is a feature, not a bug.** The user selects never-treated (stronger PT requirement: treated and never-treated would have trended alike) or not-yet-treated (weaker in one dimension, but leans on PT between later- and earlier-treated units in specific windows). No already-treated unit ever serves as a control.

**Estimation and inference.** Three routes — outcome regression, inverse probability weighting, or doubly robust AIPW — with PT allowed to hold *only conditionally on covariates*. A multiplier bootstrap delivers **simultaneous (uniform) confidence bands** across the entire event-study path, a genuine inferential advantage over pointwise intervals. Canonical application: minimum-wage effects on teen employment, 2001–2007.

**Anticipation.** Explicitly parameterized: an `anticipation` horizon δ quarantines the δ periods before adoption, requiring PT only for t ≥ g − δ and discarding potentially contaminated leads.

### 2.2 Sun–Abraham (2021): Interaction-Weighted Event Study

[*JoE* 225(2): 175–199](https://lsun20.github.io/event_studies_paper.pdf); [Stata command](https://github.com/lsun20/eventstudyinteract).

**Diagnostic first, estimator second.** SA decompose each TWFE event-study coefficient μ_ℓ and show it is a *non-convex* weighted average of cohort-specific effects CATT(e,ℓ) from its own *and other* relative periods; unless strong homogeneity holds, the cross-period terms do not cancel. The companion `eventstudyweights` command recovers these weights from an auxiliary regression on cohort shares, letting researchers quantify how large heterogeneity must be to contaminate a given coefficient.

**The fix.** Saturate the model with cohort × relative-time interactions (omitting one relative period, typically −1), estimate CATT(e,ℓ), then form the interaction-weighted estimator ν_ℓ = Σ_e CATT(e,ℓ) · Pr{E_i = e | E_i ∈ [ℓ, T̄]} — reweighting by the sample share of each cohort actually observed at horizon ℓ. Comparison group: never-treated or last-treated. Inference is pointwise (no simultaneous-band guarantee).

**Key relationship.** Sant'Anna's own teaching materials note the SA estimator *coincides numerically with CS when there are no covariates and the never-treated/last-treated cohort is the comparison group*. SA is thus best understood as the event-study-focused, regression-native cousin of CS — distinguished by its contamination diagnostic and by trivial integration into standard TWFE workflows (`fixest::feols(y ~ sunab(cohort, time) | unit + time)` in R).

### 2.3 Borusyak–Jaravel–Spiess (2024): Imputation

[*Review of Economic Studies* 91(6): 3253–3285](https://www.restud.com/revisiting-event-study-designs-robust-and-efficient-estimation/); [arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.12419); [published PDF](http://eprints.lse.ac.uk/123781/1/Jaravel_revisiting-even-study-designs--published.pdf).

**A different philosophy.** Rather than building up from 2×2 cells, BJS (i) fit unit and time fixed effects α̂_i, β̂_t by regression **using untreated observations only** (never-treated plus not-yet-treated observations of eventually-treated units); (ii) impute the counterfactual Ŷ_it(0) = α̂_i + β̂_t for every treated observation and compute τ̂_it = Y_it − Ŷ_it(0); (iii) aggregate with researcher-chosen weights to any target — event-time, calendar-time, overall ATT, or arbitrary policy-relevant summaries.

**Efficiency claim.** BJS prove this is the semiparametrically *efficient* (minimum-variance) estimator among unbiased estimators under unrestricted heterogeneity. In their simulations and tax-rebate application, confidence intervals are approximately **50% shorter than CS and 2–3.5× shorter than SA** when effects are plausibly homogeneous; efficiency gains of 20–40% over equal-weighted cohort estimators are typical. Under heterogeneity the estimator remains consistent but loses its efficiency edge. Point estimates are numerically equivalent to Gardner's two-stage estimator (`did2s`; [R Journal 2022](https://journal.r-project.org/articles/RJ-2022-048/)) and to Wooldridge's (2021) two-stage Mundlak regression ([two-stage DiD paper](https://www.bu.edu/econ/files/2024/07/two-stage-differences-in-differences.pdf)) — they differ in variance estimation. Their tax-rebate application finds a notional first-quarter MPC of 8–11%, about half the benchmark used to calibrate macro models.

**The price of efficiency.** Because stage 1 pools *all* pre-treatment periods into a global TWFE outcome model, BJS relies on the additive-separability restriction Y(0)_it = α_i + β_t holding across the entire panel — a functional-form demand the localized CS/SA comparisons do not make. If long-run cohorts and recent cohorts have differential pre-trends, the imputed counterfactuals inherit the error. This is the crisp statement of the robustness–efficiency trade-off that Marcus and Sant'Anna (*JAERE*, "The Role of Parallel Trends in Event Study Settings"; [link](https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/pdf/10.1086/711509)) formalize: different PTAs of different strengths recover different causal parameters, and practitioners "should be explicit about these trade-offs."

### 2.4 Context: the Wider Family

De Chaisemartin–D'Haultfœuille's DID_M (`did_multiplegt`) uses switchers-based Wald-DiD ratios and handles treatment reversals; Cengiz et al. (2019) "stacked" regressions build cohort-specific clean-control datasets; Dube, Girardi, Jordà and Taylor's LP-DiD ([NBER WP w31184](https://www.nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w31184/revisions/w31184.rev1.pdf)) uses local projections with a clean-control condition that "subsumes many of the recent solutions"; and Roth–Sant'Anna (2023, *JPE: Microeconomics* 1(4): 669–709; [link](https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/full/10.1086/726581)) derive the semiparametric efficiency bound under a stronger *design-based* assumption of (quasi-)random treatment timing — reaching standard-error reductions of 2× or more, and in their police-training application confidence intervals up to **8× shorter** than existing approaches. The Chiu, Lan, Liu and Xu replication study usefully taxonomizes all of this into "DID extensions" (local 2×2 building blocks: CS, SA, DID_M) versus "imputation methods" (explicit outcome models: BJS, Gardner, Wooldridge).

---

## 3. Assumption-by-Assumption Comparison

| Dimension | Callaway–Sant'Anna | Sun–Abraham | BJS / Gardner imputation | TWFE (baseline) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Parallel trends** | Generalized to all (g,t) pairs; may hold **conditionally on covariates** (OR/IPW/doubly robust); choice of never-treated (stronger) or not-yet-treated | Unconditional PT relative to never- or last-treated cohorts | PT/additive separability of Y(0) across **all** units and periods — strongest single assumption, but buys efficiency and generality | Unconditional PT |
| **Treatment-effect homogeneity** | Not required — heterogeneity is the estimand | Not required — saturated CATT(e,ℓ) free of cross-period contamination | Not required for consistency; efficiency claim derived under *unrestricted* heterogeneity | **Required** for causal interpretation (Goodman-Bacon) |
| **Anticipation** | Explicit `anticipation` horizon δ; δ pre-periods quarantined | No-anticipation maintained; handled by binning/dropping leads | No-anticipation maintained; leads excluded from post-treatment aggregation; formal assumption tests built in | Contaminates leads and lags silently |
| **Comparison group** | Never-treated **or** not-yet-treated | Never-treated or last-treated | All untreated observations pooled | Everyone — including already-treated units |
| **Base period** | Last pre-treatment period g−1 per cohort | Relative period −1 (omitted) | All pre-treatment periods via global TWFE fit | Implicit, all periods |
| **Inference** | Multiplier bootstrap, **simultaneous** bands | Pointwise CIs | Asymptotic; residual bootstrap; built-in pre-trend/placebo tests | Conventional |
| **Efficiency** | Lower (single base period, localized comparisons) | Lowest of the three in applications | Highest under correct specification (~50% shorter CIs than CS; 2–3.5× shorter than SA) | Smallest SEs — but potentially biased point estimates |
| **Data requirements** | Panel *or* repeated cross-sections; flexible covariates | Panel | Panel; extends to time-varying controls, triple differences, some non-binary treatments | Panel |
| **Software** | R `did`; Stata `csdid`/`csdid2`; Python `differences`, `diff-diff` | Stata `eventstudyinteract`; R `fixest::sunab` | Stata `did_imputation` + `event_plot`; R `didimputation` | Everything |

Three load-bearing insights from this comparison:

1. **The efficiency ordering inverts the robustness ordering.** BJS is most efficient because it borrows strength from all untreated observations under a global outcome model; CS is least efficient because each ATT(g,t) rests on a single base period and a restricted comparison set. The Boston University two-stage DiD simulation study (randomly drawn state minimum-wage laws on a 42-year panel extending Bertrand–Duflo–Mullainathan) makes the practical cost explicit: "even in cases with homogeneous treatment effects… our method yields comparable standard errors to the TWFE estimator, while **other heterogeneity-robust estimators tend to yield much larger standard errors**." Robustness is bought with precision — which is exactly why the multi-estimator norm emerged.

2. **Comparison-group choice is the main lever on PT strength, and it is a real identifying decision, not a technicality.** Never-treated comparisons require treated units to resemble a permanently untreated population; not-yet-treated comparisons require later adopters to be valid counterfactuals for earlier ones in the pre-adoption window — an assumption that fails if, e.g., late adopters anticipate or defer adoption strategically. RSBP (2023; [PDF](https://psantanna.com/files/RSBP_DiD_Review.pdf)) organize their entire practitioner checklist around making this choice explicit.

3. **Anticipation is a shared maintained assumption with different handling conventions.** CS discards the anticipation window by parameter; SA and BJS expose it in the event-study plot (negative relative-time coefficients included in pre-trend assessment, excluded from post-treatment aggregates). RSBP flag that no-anticipation is often *implicitly* violated in staggered settings — an event study with systematically negative leads is consistent with anticipation rather than pre-trends.

---

## 4. Methodological Dominance in AER/QJE/JPE, Labor and Health, 2020–2024

### 4.1 A Necessary Caveat on Evidence

No published, estimator-by-estimator bibliometric audit of AER/QJE/JPE labor- and health-economics DiD papers exists for 2020–2024. Roth (2022)'s calibration survey covers 2014–2018 (pre-adoption); Baker–Larcker–Wang cover finance and accounting; the Chiu et al. replication covers political science (102 articles, 2017–2023). The dominance assessment below is therefore a triangulation from citation data, software ecosystems, synthesis literature, field-specific guides, and named applications — high confidence in *direction*, low confidence in *magnitude*. A systematic text-mining audit in the spirit of Currie–Kleven–Zwiers remains the missing piece.

### 4.2 The Triangulated Verdict: CS Is the Modal Default Inside a Multi-Estimator Norm

**(a) Citation and software intensity.** Cunningham's package audit ([link](https://www.scunning.com/files/package_audit_r4.pdf)) reports CS at **10,750 citations in six years**, with six independent implementations — R `did`, R `ddml`, Stata `csdid`, Stata `csdid2`, Python `differences`, Python `diff-diff` — and the R `did` package at 383 GitHub stars, noting that "at this adoption scale, implementation differences affect thousands of applied papers." (RePEc/EconPapers counts for the companion papers are far lower but not comparable — RePEc systematically undercounts relative to Google Scholar.) The `did_imputation` package itself had only dozens of citations as of 2024, reflecting BJS's later formal publication.

**(b) Synthesis-paper emphasis.** In Roth, Sant'Anna, Bilinski and Poe (2023, *JoE* 235: 2218–2244; [PDF](https://www.jonathandroth.com/assets/files/DiD_Review_Paper.pdf)) — the definitive practitioner-facing synthesis — CS receives 21 mentions across 4 sections, versus Sun–Abraham 11/3, de Chaisemartin–D'Haultfœuille 7, BJS 5, Goodman-Bacon 4. The review's checklist explicitly recommends the heterogeneity-robust estimators for staggered designs, with CS as the organizing example.

**(c) The wrapper-package signal.** The `did2s`/`event_study` ecosystem runs *every* modern estimator under one syntax "allowing quick estimation and plotting of every alternative event study estimator," and Stata now ships `csdid`, `did_imputation`, `eventstudyinteract`, `did_multiplegt`, `stackedev`, `jwdid`, and `xtevent` alongside native commands. The existence of meta-packages is the clearest revealed-preference evidence that **robustness-by-multiple-estimators, not a single winner, became the applied norm**.

**(d) Field-specific patterns.** In **health economics and adjacent fields**, CS's claim is strongest: the *Annual Review of Public Health* 2024 guide "Designing Difference-in-Difference Studies with Staggered Adoption" ([link](https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-publhealth-061022-050825)) builds its checklist around CS-style estimators; epidemiology primers list CS first among heterogeneity-robust options "increasingly being implemented by epidemiologists." CS's doubly robust machinery and repeated-cross-section support suit covariate-heavy claims data. Concrete applications include Medicaid expansion replications (Rios-Avila, Sant'Anna and Callaway), PDMP mandates and employment, and COVID-19 vaccine-mandate uptake among health-care workers. In **labor economics**, where the event-study plot is the native genre, Sun–Abraham (via `fixest`'s `sunab()`) is the standard reporting device and BJS/Gardner imputation is the ascendant efficiency choice — Clemens and coauthors' minimum-wage analysis adopts `did_imputation` as its *primary* estimator, citing its "attractive properties for our setting"; CS anchors sick-pay-mandate evaluations (Pichler–Wen), noncompete studies, and the Better Work trade-program evaluation (*Economics Letters* 228, 2023).

**(e) The persistence counterweight.** The most defensible characterization sits between "CS dominance" and "no winner": CS is unambiguously the *modal* heterogeneity-robust estimator, but conventional TWFE persisted as the primary specification in a substantial share of 2020–2022 vintage papers (the critique only consolidated in late 2021), and the Chiu et al. replication of 102 articles (2017–2023, political science) found the vast majority still used TWFE, with CS the most common alternative, followed by imputation and then SA. In top-3 economics journals specifically, the transitional practice of "TWFE plus a Bacon decomposition diagnostic" remained common in 2020–2022, displaced by full robust estimators from 2022 onward. BJS's published-footprint lag is largely mechanical: the *ReStud* version is dated 2024, so its 2020–2024 influence ran through the arXiv working paper and the Stata package.

### 4.3 How Authors Justify Estimator Choice

**Monte Carlo justification by applied authors is rare; sensitivity-analysis justification is becoming standard.** The Monte Carlo evidence lives almost entirely in the methods papers: BJS's own simulation study; Gardner's Monte Carlo appendix; the BU two-stage paper's annual-state-law simulations comparing CS, SA, Wooldridge, BJS, and DID_M rejection rates. The prominent exceptions are field replication studies rather than ordinary applied papers — most notably Margolis et al. (2023, *Epidemiology*; [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1097/EDE.0000000000001611)), who compared TWFE, group-time ATT, cohort ATT, and target-trial estimators for Medicaid expansion effects on preterm birth: **TWFE estimated that expansion *increased* preterm birth risk (RD 0.12; 95% CI 0.02, 0.22), while the group-time ATT, cohort ATT, and target-trial approaches estimated protective or null effects** — a vivid, health-economics-native demonstration of sign reversal under heterogeneity, confirmed in their simulations ("two-way fixed effects performed well when treatment effects were constant and less well under heterogeneous and dynamic effects").

The dominant justification pattern in AER/QJE/JPE applied work is instead: (i) cite Goodman-Bacon/de Chaisemartin–D'Haultfœuille/Sun–Abraham for the critique; (ii) report a heterogeneity-robust primary estimate (usually CS) with a second estimator (SA event study or imputation) as robustness — the "if all three agree, results are robust; if they disagree, investigate heterogeneity" heuristic from the `diff-diff` tutorials; and (iii) increasingly after 2023, append a Rambachan–Roth HonestDiD sensitivity analysis with a breakdown value M̄. Formal justification of the *choice among* robust estimators via first-principles argument (comparison-group plausibility, covariate availability, efficiency needs) appears in the stronger papers; bespoke simulation studies do not.

---

## 5. Roth (2022) and the Pre-Trend Problem: What the New Estimators Fix and What They Don't

### 5.1 The Critique

Roth, "Pretest with Caution: Event-Study Estimates after Testing for Parallel Trends," *AER: Insights* 4(3): 305–322 ([link](https://www.aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257/aeri.20210236); [longer version](https://www.jonathandroth.com/assets/files/roth_pretrends_testing_longer_version.pdf)), calibrates simulations to his survey of **70 papers published in three leading economics journals (AER/QJE/JPE) between 2014 and 2018** that display event-study plots, and documents two failures of conventional pre-trend testing:

1. **Low power.** Conventional pre-tests have only ~50% power against linear pre-trend violations that would produce bias *comparable in magnitude to the estimated treatment effect*. A non-significant lead coefficient is close to uninformative against economically relevant violations.
2. **Pre-test bias from conditioning.** Data draws that survive the pre-test are a selected sample. Conditional on passing, conventional 95% confidence intervals fail to cover the true average post-treatment effect roughly **half the time in the median paper**, and the conditional bias can exceed **twice** the unconditional bias — in non-pathological cases, "fixing" the design on a passed pre-test makes things worse.

### 5.2 Mechanism 1 — Sun–Abraham Removes *Spurious* Pre-Trends

SA's central result — "apparent pretrends can arise solely from treatment effects heterogeneity" — means a TWFE event-study lead coefficient is not merely low-powered; it is *affirmatively misleading*, because large post-treatment effects in early cohorts contaminate estimated leads for later cohorts. "Any test of μ_ℓ = 0 cannot accept or reject the existence of pretrends without further assumptions on treatment effects." The IW estimator produces pre-period coefficients that are actually interpretable as pre-trends, and `eventstudyweights` quantifies how much heterogeneity would be needed to manufacture a given apparent pre-trend. This addresses the *validity of the object being tested*, not the power of the test.

### 5.3 Mechanism 2 — BJS Separates Estimation from Testing

BJS's pre-trend/placebo test is constructed from the stage-1 fit on untreated observations only, comparing imputed versus actual pre-period outcomes. Because the treatment-effect estimates are computed independently of the test, "this approach avoids the contamination of the tests by treatment-effect heterogeneity shown by Sun and Abraham (2021). Moreover, our strategy circumvents the inference problems after pre-testing that were pointed out by Roth (2022)." **Important qualification:** this circumvention result holds *under spherical errors* — the clean statistical separation of testing and estimation relies on that error structure, so the guarantee is weaker under the arbitrary within-unit autocorrelation typical of applied panels. CS instead offers a joint Wald pre-test across *all* pre-treatment group-time cells with a multiplicity correction, integrated with the simultaneous-band bootstrap — a better test statistic, but still subject to Roth's power and conditioning critique if used as a binary gate.

### 5.4 Mechanism 3 — Power-Aware Diagnostics and Sensitivity Analysis (the Real Answer)

The literature's substantive response to Roth (2022) is a pair of complements that the new estimators plug into:

- **Power/equivalence diagnostics.** RSBP (2023) recommend "accompanying the event-study plot with diagnostics of the power of the pre-test against relevant alternatives and/or non-inferiority tests." Roth's `pretrends` R package ([GitHub](https://github.com/jonathandroth/pretrends)) computes the *minimum detectable violation* at given power — the MDE logic imported from RCT power analysis — so a researcher can state what the pre-test *could* have detected rather than treating "insignificant" as "absent."
- **Rambachan–Roth (2023), "A More Credible Approach to Parallel Trends," *ReStud* 90(5): 2555–2591** ([link](https://www.restud.com/a-more-credible-approach-to-parallel-trends/); [PDF](https://www.jonathandroth.com/assets/files/HonestParallelTrends_Main.pdf)). Instead of testing whether parallel trends holds exactly, impose restrictions on *how large* post-treatment violations can be relative to pre-treatment ones: **relative-magnitudes restrictions (Δ^RM)** bound the post-period violation by M̄ times the maximal pre-period violation; **smoothness restrictions (Δ^SD)** bound the violation's evolution via second differences. The causal parameter is partially identified with *uniformly valid* confidence intervals, delivered by the `HonestDiD` R/Stata packages ([CRAN](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/HonestDiD/refman/HonestDiD.html)). Reporting the **breakdown value** — the smallest M̄ at which the conclusion overturns — converts pre-trend assessment from a binary pass/fail ritual into a quantitative robustness statement. Sant'Anna maintains a `CS_RR` repository wiring `did` directly into `HonestDiD`, which is itself evidence that the sensitivity layer is designed to sit *on top of* the heterogeneity-robust estimators rather than replace them.

### 5.5 The Emergent Standard Workflow

The de facto 2023–2024 best-practice stack for staggered DiD in labor and health applications — visible in the Medicaid-expansion replication literature and codified in the RSBP checklist — is: (i) report TWFE alongside a heterogeneity-robust primary estimate (usually CS, with a Goodman-Bacon decomposition as diagnostic); (ii) present a Sun–Abraham IW event-study plot; (iii) report a *joint* pre-trend test with a power diagnostic or minimum-detectable-violation statement; and (iv) report an HonestDiD M̄ breakdown value. Roth's critique has thus reshaped the evidentiary standard not by eliminating pre-trend assessment but by demoting it from a gatekeeping hypothesis test to one component of a documented sensitivity analysis.

---

## 6. Bottom Line

1. **Common core, different mechanics.** CS (group-time ATTs, base period g−1, never- or not-yet-treated controls, conditional-PT/doubly-robust estimation, simultaneous bootstrap bands), SA (saturated cohort × relative-time interactions with cohort-share reweighting — numerically equivalent to CS without covariates under never-treated comparison), and BJS/Gardner (imputation on untreated observations using all pre-periods, semiparametric efficiency, ~50% shorter CIs than CS at the price of a global outcome-model assumption) all eliminate forbidden

# Acadia Realty Trust (AKR): Capital Allocation and Risk Management Across the Portfolio Transformation

**Bottom line:** Acadia's evolving portfolio strategy demonstrates effective — though not costless — capital allocation. The Core Portfolio is a structurally higher-quality earnings stream than the Funds segment (Q1 2024 operating margin of 32.4% vs. 17.0%), and management is rationally converting passive minority fund positions into controlling, consolidated ownership of high-barrier street retail, exemplified by the January 2025 Renaissance Portfolio step-up (20% → 68% for $117.9M cash against $245.7M gross value with $156.1M of assumed debt). The 2025 impairment cluster — $37.2M consolidated across Fund III and Fund IV assets, 100% triggered by "reduced holding period" — is best read as a deliberate, rapidly monetized harvest of legacy fund vintages rather than operating distress, with only ~$8.9M (24%) of the gross charge borne by Acadia. The ~$315–325M 2025 consolidated debt increase (term loan plus Renaissance consolidation) was substantially equity-funded via ~$278M of settled ATM forwards, and pro-rata leverage *improved* from 6.3–6.6x to 4.9x (adjusted) / 5.6x (unadjusted) — evidence of an expansionary-but-disciplined balance sheet, not capital constraint. The pattern reveals genuine management confidence in the dual-platform transformation, with the principal residual risks being further fund-vintage marks (City Point remains a ~$553M residual Funds asset) and dependence on sustained Core same-store NOI growth (5.7% in Q1 2024, >5% for twelve consecutive quarters) to service the enlarged debt load.

---

## 1. Baseline Business Quality: Q1 2024 Segment Operating Margins

From the Q1 2024 10-Q segment disclosure ([SEC EDGAR R92](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/899629/000095017024050536/R92.htm)):

| Three months ended March 31, 2024 | Core Portfolio | Opportunity Funds |
|---|---|---|
| Total revenues | $53,538K | $37,818K |
| Property operating expenses & RE taxes | $(17,919)K | $(13,523)K |
| Depreciation & amortization | $(18,267)K | $(16,673)K |
| Loss on previously disposed property | — | $(1,198)K |
| **Operating income** | **$17,352K** | **$6,424K** |
| **Operating margin** | **32.4%** | **17.0%** |
| NOI-type margin ((Rev − PropOpEx)/Rev) | 66.5% | 64.2% |
| D&A intensity (D&A/Rev) | 34.1% | 44.1% |

**Key analytical insight:** The 15.4-percentage-point operating margin gap is *not* a property-operations story — NOI margins are nearly identical (66.5% vs. 64.2%). The divergence is driven almost entirely by (a) the Funds' heavier depreciation burden (44.1% of revenue vs. 34.1%) and (b) $1.2M of disposition-related loss noise in the Funds segment. This is a structural feature of the value-add fund model, not an operational deficiency: shorter holds, intensive repositioning, and front-loaded capitalized costs inflate D&A relative to current earnings, with returns harvested at exit (the same segment recorded a ~$25.0M realized/unrealized gain in Q1 2023).

**Deteriorating trend within Funds:** The margin gap widened from 8.3 points in Q1 2023 (Core 30.2% vs. Funds 21.9%) to 15.4 points in Q1 2024. Funds revenue grew ~18% year-over-year yet operating income *fell* from ~$7.0M to $6.4M — incremental Funds revenue generated negative marginal profit, while Core revenue grew 7.5% with expanding margins. The Funds segment also still carried significant residual asset mass (City Point in Fund II alone was ~$553.4M of the segment's ~$1.6B in assets).

**Implication:** The baseline establishes exactly why the strategic pivot makes sense. Core street/open-air retail converts NOI into operating profit roughly 1.9x more efficiently than the fund platform. Capital allocation that shifts the mix toward controlled Core assets — and harvests legacy fund positions — targets the higher-quality earnings stream. ([Q1 2024 10-Q segment note](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/899629/000095017024050536/R92.htm))

---

## 2. Renaissance Portfolio: Net Cash Investment and the Controlling-Interest Thesis

**Transaction (closed January 23, 2025;** [FY2025 10-K Note 2](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/899629/000119312526051677/R16.htm)):

| Parameter | Amount |
|---|---|
| Purchase price for additional 48% economic interest | **$117.9M cash** |
| Resulting ownership | 20% → **68%** (controlling financial interest; consolidation triggered) |
| Gross portfolio fair value | $245.7M |
| Existing mortgage debt assumed (venture level) | $156.1M |
| Implied underlying equity value ($245.7M − $156.1M) | **$89.6M** |
| Portfolio LTV at acquisition | 63.5% |
| Loss on change in control (remeasurement of prior 20% equity-method stake) | **$9.6M non-cash** |

**Net cash/equity investment calculation:** The $117.9M price equals 48% × $245.7M — i.e., priced on *gross asset value*. Because the $156.1M mortgage remained in the venture, Acadia's effective net equity outlay was $117.9M − (48% × $156.1M = $74.9M) = **~$43.0M**, exactly 48% of the implied $89.6M equity value. There was no overpayment; the headline price simply grosses up for the debt that attaches to the acquired interest. Consolidation placed the full $245.7M asset base and $156.1M debt on Acadia's balance sheet, with a 32% noncontrolling interest carve-out to the partner (EastBanc).

**Immediate financing optimization (January 24, 2025 — one day post-close):** The venture modified the assumed mortgage (maturing November 6, 2026), cutting the spread from **SOFR + 2.65% to SOFR + 1.55%** — a ~110 bps reduction — via a **~$50.0M principal paydown funded by Acadia as an intercompany note receivable** (9.11% coupon, November 2026 maturity, eliminated in consolidation). (Two panel sources corroborate $50.0M per the 10-K; a third describes a $54.1M paydown funded through a $57.1M note including ~$3.0M of capitalized costs — likely different descriptions of the same transaction, with $50M the better-corroborated figure.) A subsequent 2025 paydown was structured so the 32% noncontrolling partner funded its proportionate share.

**Strategic alignment — this is the controlling-interest strategy executed in textbook form:**
1. **Control conversion:** Acadia moved from a passive 20% equity-method position (generating only ~$2.1M of equity in earnings in Q1 2024) to a 68% consolidated stake with direct control over leasing and operations of a trophy asset — the Georgetown Renaissance Collection: 36 retail stores across 20 buildings, 318,000+ sq. ft. along M Street, one of the nation's premier street-retail corridors.
2. **Earnings-quality upgrade:** The portfolio's NOI migrates from the fee-driven fund/equity-method channel into the segment with the 32.4% operating margin.
3. **Cost-of-capital arbitrage:** Acadia deployed corporate capital to strip ~110 bps off third-party debt cost; 68% of the resulting NOI uplift accrues to Acadia shareholders.

**Honest caveats:** The $9.6M change-in-control loss signals that the prior carrying value of the 20% stake exceeded fair value — prior marks were optimistic. And the 9.11% intercompany note rate is anomalous: one reading (minority view) is that needing to fund the paydown internally at a double-digit rate, rather than refinancing externally at market, hints at asset-level financing friction. The better-corroborated reading is that the note is eliminated in consolidation and functions as a deliberate balance-sheet retention tool — Acadia captures the rate reduction's benefit rather than ceding it to an outside lender — but the internal rate's premium to Acadia's own consolidated borrowing cost (~4.6% on the new term loan) is a real data point worth monitoring.

---

## 3. Impairment Concentration and Timing: Fund III, Fund IV, and Bald Hill Road

**The 2025 impairment cluster** ([FY2025 10-K Note 8, nonrecurring fair value measurements](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/899629/000119312526051677/R85.htm)):

| Property | Fund | Trigger | Measurement date | Gross charge | Acadia share | Outcome |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| New York, NY (640 Broadway) | Fund III | Reduced holding period | June 30, 2025 | $7,240K | $1,777K | Sold Q3 2025 for $49.5M |
| 1035 Third Avenue, New York, NY | Fund IV | Reduced holding period | June 30, 2025 | $17,400K | $3,991K | Sold October 2025 for $22.0M |
| Broad Hollow Commons, East Farmingdale, NY | Fund III | Reduced holding period | Sept 30, 2025 | $12,570K | $3,085K | Marked to $21.3M FV (10% discount / 7% cap); transferred out of development |
| **Consolidated 2025 total** | | | | **$37,210K** | **$8,853K** | |
| 650 Bald Hill Road, Warwick, RI (unconsolidated JV; 20.81% interest) | Fund IV | Shortened holding period | 2025 | ~$3,500K venture-level | ~$700K | Sold April 2026 for $20.5M (Acadia share ~$4.3M) |

**Prior-year baseline:** 2024 impairments totaled just **$1.678M** (1964 Union Street, San Francisco — Fund IV, $1.17M; plus Mark Plaza, Edwardsville, PA — Core, $0.51M, triggered by reduced projected NOI) ([FY2024 fair value disclosure](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/899629/000095017025021145/R84.htm)); 2023 totaled **$3.686M** (146 Geary Street, San Francisco — Fund IV). The 2025 surge to ~$40.7M (including Bald Hill) is a roughly **24x year-over-year increase**.

**Concentration analysis:**
- **Single trigger:** 100% of the consolidated 2025 fund impairments cite "reduced/shortened holding period" — a strategic exit-timing signal, not tenant or NOI distress.
- **Temporal clustering:** ~60.5% of gross charges were effective June 30, 2025 and ~30.9% effective September 30, 2025 — a deliberate six-month recognition window consistent with a board-level disposition decision.
- **Geographic/fund clustering:** Two NYC properties account for $24.6M (~66%) of the consolidated total; Fund III bears $19.8M (~49%) and Fund IV $17.4M (~43%) of gross charges.
- **Valuation realism:** The marks embed a materially higher cost of capital — 10.0% discount / 7.0% cap (East Farmingdale) and 9.25% discount / 8.25% cap (NYC Fund IV) — reflecting mid-2025 rate conditions.
- **Risk distribution:** Of the $37.2M gross consolidated charge, Acadia's net burden was only **~$8.9M (24%)**; fund limited partners and OP unitholders absorbed the remaining ~$28.4M — a structural benefit of the fund vehicle during wind-down.
- **Rapid monetization:** Roughly $44.6M of cumulative gross charges converted to actual cash realizations within 4–7 months of recognition (640 Broadway, 1035 Third Avenue, and — in April 2026 — Bald Hill Road at $20.5M) ([Q1 2026 supplemental](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/899629/000119312526321040/akr-ex99_2.htm)). Accounting marks were near-immediately validated by market-clearing sales.

**Bald Hill Road specifics:** As an unconsolidated Fund IV JV asset (20.81% interest), the impairment flowed through **equity in (losses) earnings of unconsolidated affiliates** rather than the consolidated impairment line; the 10-K attributes the Investment Management segment's ~$20.3M year-over-year deterioration in equity earnings primarily to the Bald Hill impairment together with the Eden Square disposition loss ([FY2025 10-K MD&A](https://ebs.publicnow.com/view/EE8EDFEA11ACAA12918AE30A54605A03578B9E86)). Bald Hill — a Warwick, RI asset outside the core street-retail thesis — is the cleanest example of pruning a non-strategic position at acceptable economics.

**Risk interpretation:** The pattern reveals the genuine cost of the fund-exit mechanism: when management accelerates realization timelines for legacy Fund III/IV vintages (Fund V's investment period closed August 2023), carrying values built on longer-hold assumptions prove unsustainable, and impairments arrive in concentrated waves. The clustering across two funds and one metro suggests prior valuations were systematically optimistic on NYC fund assets. However, this is the *mechanical consequence of the announced pivot* — the 2025 Annual Report states the platform has "evolved… away from traditional single closed end funds toward a more flexible multi-channel joint venture structure" ([2025 Annual Report](https://acadiarealty.com/wp-content/uploads/2025_Annual_Report.pdf)) — and the economics of the broader harvest remain strong (the Fund V recapitalization returned an 18% IRR and 1.9x equity multiple to LPs). The shortened-hold-period trigger is a strategy signal; the residual risk is that further vintage assets (e.g., City Point) require similar marks before the wind-down completes.

---

## 4. The 2025 Net Debt Increase: Value Creation or Capital Constraint?

**The two financing moves:**

1. **$250M delayed-draw term loan (Q2 2025)** — established via the Third Amendment to the Credit Agreement dated May 29, 2025 ([Ex-10.1](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/899629/000095017025100264/akr-ex10_1.htm); [Q2 2025 earnings release](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/899629/000095017025099653/akr-ex99_1.htm)): $175M drawn at closing with $75M of remaining capacity; **SOFR + 120 bps; ~4.6% all-in effective rate inclusive of interest-rate swaps**; five-year term; proceeds repaid revolver borrowings and a secured obligation; accordion capacity increased to **$1.5 billion**.
2. **Renaissance mortgage paydown (January 24, 2025):** the ~$50M internal paydown described above, cutting the assumed loan's spread by ~110 bps.

**Debt trajectory (the full picture, including the prior-year deleveraging that reframes everything):**

| Date | Consolidated debt | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Dec 31, 2023 | ~$1,881M | Pre-deleveraging peak |
| Dec 31, 2024 | **$1,547.9M** gross carrying value | ~$333M deleveraging during 2024 |
| Dec 31, 2025 | **$1,873.4M** gross carrying value ($1,862.9M principal) | **+$325M gross / +$315M principal** |

The ~$315–325M 2025 increase (term loan drawdown + consolidation of the Renaissance mortgage net of paydowns + ordinary-course activity, offset by repayments including a $50M property mortgage payoff and ~$4.5M scheduled amortization) essentially *restores* debt to its 2023 level after a full year of deleveraging — this is repositioning, not stress. ([Q4 2025 supplemental](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/899629/000119312526044722/akr-ex99_2.htm))

**The leverage ratio fell even as gross debt rose:**

| Date | Pro-rata Net Debt / EBITDA |
|---|---|
| Mar 31, 2024 | 6.6x |
| Jun 30, 2024 | 6.3x |
| Mar 31, 2025 | 5.7x |
| Jun 30, 2025 | 5.5x |
| Sep 30, 2025 | 5.0x |
| Dec 31, 2025 | **5.6x (Net Debt/EBITDA); 4.9x (Net Debt/Adjusted EBITDA); 5.2x ex-realized gains** |

Net Debt + Preferred / Total Market Capitalization stood at just **27%** at year-end 2025. Pro-rata net debt was $1,154.2M against $1,494.7M of pro-rata total debt capitalization.

**The critical equity offset:** The debt increase was predominantly equity-funded. Acadia settled **11.2M ATM forward shares in Q1 2025 for ~$277.5M of net proceeds**, and held **14.7M unsettled forward shares worth ~$295.5M** at December 31, 2025. Combined with ~$525M of revolver availability and ~$45M of cash, total dry powder exceeded **$800M** against an announced ~$445M YTD 2026 acquisition pipeline and the Henderson Avenue redevelopment. There are no significant REIT Portfolio debt maturities until 2028–29.

**Verdict — value creation, not capital constraint:**
- The term loan is **accretive and duration-extending**: 4.6% all-in swapped fixed-equivalent cost replacing shorter-tenor revolver/secured debt, pushing maturities to ~2030 and expanding accordion capacity to $1.5B — a balance sheet being shaped for offense.
- **Leverage improved ~140–170 bps** (6.3–6.6x → 4.9x adjusted) over 18 months because EBITDA growth, asset sales, and forward equity expanded the denominator and equity base faster than debt grew.
- The Renaissance paydown was **voluntary optimization**, not forced deleveraging — Acadia *added* a $50M note receivable and retained control rather than surrendering economics.
- The minority counter-signal (the 9.11% intercompany rate) is worth flagging but is overwhelmed by the external evidence: a REIT under capital constraint does not upsize its accordion to $1.5B, draw term debt at SOFR+120, settle $278M of equity forwards at accretive prices, and simultaneously fund $445M of acquisitions.

**The cost side of the ledger:** consolidated interest expense rose to ~$95.3M in FY2025 (vs. ~$85.9M annualized from Q1 2024). Servicing that load comfortably requires the Core same-store NOI engine — +5.7% in Q1 2024, above 5% for twelve consecutive quarters — to keep compounding. That dependence is the strategy's central execution risk.

---

## 5. Synthesis: What This Reveals About Management's Confidence

The four analyses interlock into a coherent transformation narrative:

1. **Business quality justified the pivot.** The Core Portfolio's 32.4% operating margin vs. the Funds' 17.0% — with the gap *widening* year-over-year — gave management a quantified mandate to shift the mix toward controlled Core/REIT assets and institutional joint ventures (TPG for LINQ Promenade; Cohen & Steers for Highwoods Preserve).
2. **Capital is following the stated strategy with precision.** The Renaissance step-up converted a passive 20% stake into 68% control of premier Georgetown street retail at an implied $43.0M net equity outlay, immediately optimized via a ~110 bps debt-cost reduction — despite absorbing a $9.6M non-cash remeasurement loss to do so. Paying a known accounting cost to obtain control is a confidence signal, not a retreat.
3. **Impairments are the planned cost of exit, executed with discipline.** A single trigger (shortened hold periods), tight temporal clustering, rapid conversion to cash sales, and a 76% risk-transfer to fund LPs all indicate deliberate harvesting of Fund III/IV vintages — with Bald Hill Road pruning the non-strategic unconsolidated tail. The transparency and speed of the mark-to-sale cycle (4–7 months) argues against impairment concealment.
4. **The balance sheet is being used as a strategic tool.** A ~$315–325M gross debt increase that nonetheless *improves* leverage to 4.9x (adjusted), extends maturities to 2029+, and leaves $800M+ of liquidity is expansionary financing executed from strength.

**Overall assessment:** Effective capital allocation and risk management, with confidence corroborated by actions (equity issuance, accordion upsizing, control acquisitions) rather than merely asserted. The transformation's proof points still ahead: (a) completing the fund wind-down — City Point's ~$553M gross asset value in particular — without further material marks; (b) sustaining Core NOI growth above the rate at which interest expense grows; and (c) demonstrating that consolidated Renaissance economics validate the $9.6M change-in-control cost. Watch items that current disclosures don't fully resolve: FFO/AFFO-per-share accretion from the pivot, fund-level DPI/TVPI for the harvesting vintages, peer-relative leverage (street-retail peers such as Federal Realty and Kite Realty typically trade in a similar 5–6x band, making AKR's 4.9–5.6x unremarkable but not conservative), and forward Core capex needs on newly consolidated legacy assets.

---

**Primary sources:** [Q1 2024 10-Q segment data](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/899629/000095017024050536/R92.htm) · [FY2025 10-K Note 2 (Renaissance)](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/899629/000119312526051677/R16.htm) · [FY2025 10-K Note 8 (impairments)](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/899629/000119312526051677/R85.htm) · [FY2024 impairment disclosure](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/899629/000095017025021145/R84.htm) · [Term loan amendment (Ex-10.1)](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/899629/000095017025100264/akr-ex10_1.htm) · [Q2 2025 earnings release](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/899629/000095017025099653/akr-ex99_1.htm) · [Q4 2025 supplemental](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/899629/000119312526044722/akr-ex99_2.htm) · [Q1 2026 supplemental (Bald Hill sale)](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/899629/000119312526321040/akr-ex99_2.htm) · [FY2025 10-K MD&A](https://ebs.publicnow.com/view/EE8EDFEA11ACAA12918AE30A54605A03578B9E86) · [2025 Annual Report](https://acadiarealty.com/wp-content/uploads/2025_Annual_Report.pdf)

# Multi-Tasking Machine Selection for Ti-6Al-4V Aerospace Machining — Nuevo León, Mexico

**DMG MORI NLX 2500SY vs. Mazak Integrex i-400S vs. Okuma Multus U4000**

---

## 0. First, Resolve the Utilization Figure — It Changes the Whole Decision

A calendar year contains **8,760 hours** (24 × 365). A stated requirement of 15,000 annual hours is **1.71× the physical maximum for one machine** — it cannot be a single-machine figure. Before any cost model or machine comparison is valid, restate the requirement. Realistic interpretations:

| Scenario | Available hr/machine/yr | Machines needed for 15,000 hr |
|---|---|---|
| 2 shifts × 8 h × 250 days | ~4,000 | 15,000 ÷ 4,000 ≈ **4 machines** |
| 3 shifts × 8 h × 250 days | ~6,000 | 15,000 ÷ 6,000 ≈ **3 machines** |
| 24/7 with 85% availability | ~7,446 | ~2 machines (extreme duty) |
| Twin-spindle logging (spindle-hours, not machine-hours) | up to ~17,500 spindle-hr theoretical | 1–2 machines |

The two most defensible readings: **(1) fleet-level demand** across 2–4 machines at 4,000–6,000 hr each, or **(2) spindle-hours** (a twin-spindle machine logs roughly 2× clock hours). Note that sustained operation beyond ~6,000 hr/yr on a single machine is "extreme duty" that accelerates spindle wear dramatically — which makes the **DMG MORI 36-month unlimited-spindle-hours warranty** ([NLX 2500 2nd Gen](https://en.dmgmori.com/products/machines/turning/universal-turning/nlx/nlx-2500-2nd)) a uniquely valuable hedge under high-utilization assumptions. **Recommendation: size the fleet at 3–4 machines under a 2- or 3-shift model, standardize on one platform, and evaluate all three candidates on per-machine-hour economics.** The comparison below is per machine; fleet sizing follows from your shift plan.

---

## 1. Direct Recommendation

There is no single winner — the correct choice depends on dominant work mix:

- **Chucked titanium shafts, flanges, and mill-turn-dominated parts:** **DMG MORI NLX 2500SY (2nd Gen)** — best continuous turning torque with the 12" spindle option (1,273 Nm), documented 7 µm radial thermal stability in continuous operation, the deepest Siemens NX CAM integration of the three (vendor-certified MTSK postprocessor + CSE simulation + DMG MORI technology cycles in NX), OPC-UA/MTConnect/MQTT standard, and the only unlimited-spindle-hours warranty (36 months).
- **Large, heavy prismatic titanium structural parts in DONE-IN-ONE setups:** **Mazak Integrex i-400S** — highest peak main-spindle torque (~1,400 Nm at 25% ED), heaviest structure (16,200 kg), largest envelope. **Caveat: verify production status in writing — the i-400S is flagged as a discontinued model in machine-tool listing databases; the current Integrex i NEO with MAZATROL SmoothAi may be the quotable successor.** Also confirm which spindle package is quoted, as Mazak documentation shows both 1,400 Nm (25% ED) and 500 Nm (40% ED) variants.
- **Mixed shaft + 5-axis contour work in a non-climate-controlled shop:** **Okuma Multus U4000** — the most independently validated thermal stability (Thermo-Friendly Concept, JSME award; published X 7 µm / Y 8 µm / Z 9 µm displacement over an 8 °C ambient swing), strongest milling-oriented B-axis head (25/19 kW, 120 Nm, Capto C6), 300 mm Y-axis travel, single-source manufacturing (Okuma builds its own spindles, motors, encoders, and control — lowest 10–15-year obsolescence risk), and the only **AS9100D-certified service partner** in the region (HEMAQ Monterrey, 4,000+ Okuma installations since 1989).

For a **mixed-job titanium shop**, the **Okuma Multus U4000 with the high-torque/big-bore spindle option (955 Nm)** is the most balanced single-platform answer.

---

## 2. Spindle Torque and Rigidity

⚠️ **Rating conventions differ between builders and are NOT directly comparable** (25% ED vs. 30-min vs. 20-min vs. 10-min vs. continuous). Quoted with stated duty cycles:

| Parameter | DMG MORI NLX 2500SY (2nd Gen) | Mazak Integrex i-400S | Okuma Multus U4000 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Main spindle speed | 5,000 rpm (10"); 3,000 rpm (12" opt.) | 3,300 rpm | 4,200 rpm std; 3,000 rpm big-bore |
| Main spindle torque | 843 Nm (10"); **1,273 Nm (12" opt.)** | **1,400 Nm @ 25% ED** (~1,032 ft-lb); ~800 Nm continuous | 700/477 Nm (30-min/cont) std; **955/657 Nm (10-min/cont) high-output/big-bore** |
| Main spindle power | 26 kW (10") / 36 kW (12") | 30 kW (30-min) / 22 kW cont | 22/15 kW std; 32/22 kW big-bore |
| Milling/rotary spindle | BMT60: 86–100 Nm @ 12,000 rpm, 13/10 kW | Capto C6: **120 Nm, 22 kW @ 12,000 rpm** (20k opt.) | H1 B-axis: **120/90 Nm, 25/19 kW @ 12,000 rpm**, Capto C6 |
| Sub/second spindle | up to 577 Nm (10", Gen 2) | ~500 Nm class (one source lists ~800 Nm — confirm quoted package) | ~420 Nm class |
| Y-axis travel | ±50–60 mm | ±130 mm | **±150 mm (300 mm)** |
| Machine mass | ~6.4 t | **16.2 t** | ~14 t class |
| Work envelope | ø366 mm × 708–1,258 mm | ø658 mm × 1,519 mm | ø650 mm × 1,500–2,000 mm |

Sources: [DMG MORI NLX 2500 2nd Gen](https://en.dmgmori.com/products/machines/turning/universal-turning/nlx/nlx-2500-2nd); [Okuma MULTUS U Series brochure, Jun 2025](https://www.okuma.com/files/documents/MULTUS-U-Series_Jun2025-P500.pdf); [Mazak Integrex i-400S listings/spec sheet](https://cnc-toerner.de/pt/maschine/mazak-integrex-i-400-s-18/), [machinetoolindex.com](https://www.machinetoolindex.com).

**Rigidity engineering:**
- **DMG MORI:** FEM-analyzed bed with claimed 30% higher rigidity than the prior series; box slideways plus 55 mm roller guides; double-anchored, internally cooled ball screws; documented spindle labyrinth and air-purge designed for frequent high-pressure-coolant use — a durability detail directly relevant to titanium chip evacuation ([NLX brochure via Lister](https://www.listermachinetools.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/09/pt0uk-nlx2500nd-pdf-data.pdf)).
- **Mazak:** mass-based damping strategy; 16.2 t is the best static-stiffness proxy of the three and the best fit for chatter-prone low-frequency Ti roughing.
- **Okuma:** diagonal-rib bed castings ("7× the rigidity" vs. non-ribbed structure, per Okuma) with orthogonal traveling-column feed — designed for stable cutting across the full Y range.

**Analysis for Ti-6Al-4V:** titanium roughing runs at 30–60 m/min with high cutting forces and heat concentrated at the tool tip; what matters is **low-speed torque and damping, not top rpm**. The i-400S leads peak torque and mass; the NLX 2500 Gen 2 with the 12" option leads continuous torque *within its size class* — but note the NLX is fundamentally a size class smaller (ø366 mm vs. ø650–658 mm swing) and is a turning-mill rather than a full multitasking center (its ≤100 Nm BMT milling drive is not a substitute for the Mazak/Okuma B-axis spindles on prismatic work). The Multus U4000's high-output option (955 Nm) plus the strongest milling head makes it the best *mill-heavy* compromise.

---

## 3. Tooling for Ti-6Al-4V — Ceramic Limitations Are Decisive

**Exclude alumina-based and SiC-whisker ceramics from the Ti-6Al-4V tooling library entirely.** The literature is unambiguous:

> "Silicon carbide whisker reinforced (WG 300 grade) alumina ceramic tools are not suitable for machining titanium alloys… due to the accelerated tool wear and chipping/fracture of the cutting edge associated with chemical interactions between the ceramic tools and titanium alloys." — [Comparative Analysis of SiAlON, CBN and Carbide for Titanium Machining (2024)](https://www.academia.edu/114605495/Comparative_Analysis_of_the_Cutting_Performances_of_SiAlON_Ceramic_Cubic_Boron_Nitride_and_Carbide_Cutting_Tools_for_Titanium_Machining)

- Al₂O₃/TiCN ceramics show "coating peel-off and tool flaking… due to thermal instability at higher cutting speeds" and elevated friction/temperature at the tool tip ([*Sadhana*/IASc 2022](https://www.ias.ac.in/article/fulltext/sadh/047/0105)).
- "Ceramic inserts were also not suitable for single point turning of titanium alloys" ([Khan 2024, Univ. of Greenwich repository](https://gala.gre.ac.uk/id/eprint/48453)); CBN likewise fails economically via severe chipping ([Scientific.Net/AMR](https://doi.org/10.4028/www.scientific.net/amr.1135.234)).
- In a comparative face-milling RSM study on Ti-6Al-4V, carbide outperformed both SiAlON and CBN on tool life ([Springer IJA-MT 2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00170-024-13225-3)).

**Practical tooling specification (material constraint — applies equally to all three machines):**

| Class | Verdict for Ti-6Al-4V |
|---|---|
| Fine-grain uncoated or **PVD-coated WC-Co carbide (AlTiN / AlCrN)**, sharp positive geometry | **Recommended baseline** (AlTiN maximizes tool life in micro/profile milling — [PMC/NIH coated micro end mill study](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6267563/)) |
| SiAlON ceramic | Marginal at best, only with high-pressure coolant at moderate speeds; elevated fracture risk |
| Al₂O₃ / SiC-whisker ceramic | **Do not use** — chemical reactivity, chipping |
| CBN | Not recommended — rapid wear, no economic benefit |
| PCD | Niche finishing option only (up to ~250 m/min with HPC); too brittle for interrupted cuts |

**High-pressure coolant (HPC) is the single highest-leverage productivity enabler:** directed jets at 70–300 bar reduce tool-tip temperature ~25% and flank wear up to ~50% ([SAGE Proc. IMechE](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/09544054JEM2082)); through-insert coolant (e.g., Kennametal Beyond Blast) doubled tool life vs. flood in Ti turning ([MMS Online](https://www.mmsonline.com/articles/a-systems-approach-for-successful-titanium-machining)). Note diminishing/negative returns at excessive pressure (60 bar matched 140+ bar without edge-blast damage). **Machine implication:** since ceramics (which demand high-rpm capability) are off the table, prioritize low-speed torque, damping, and factory HPC provision. Budget **$30–60k per machine installed** for HPC plumbing as a hidden CAPEX line, and verify HPC as a line item on the Mazak and Okuma quotations (DMG MORI documents HPC-ready spindle sealing explicitly).

---

## 4. Thermal Compensation for ±0.0005" (±12.7 µm)

This tolerance is at the outer edge of what any of the three can hold **without** active thermal compensation. Published, quantified performance differs meaningfully:

- **Okuma Multus U4000 — Thermo-Friendly Concept (TAS-S spindle + TAS-C structure).** Most fully documented system, recipient of a JSME award. Symmetric "manageable deformation" design plus sensor-driven real-time compensation: published displacement of **X 7 µm (⌀13 µm), Y 8 µm, Z 9 µm over an 8 °C ambient change**, with suppressed column/spindle tilt, no warm-up cycle required, and stability claimed "in normal factory environments with no special measures" ([Okuma brochure](https://www.okuma.com/files/documents/MULTUS-U-Series_Jun2025-P500.pdf); [Okuma Thermo-Friendly](https://www.okuma.co.jp/english/solution_technology/thermo)). OSP-P500 adds 0.1 µm control resolution, AbsoScale glass-scale feedback, and Accuracy Stability Diagnosis. For a Monterrey-area shop facing ~5–40 °C seasonal swings without full climate control, this is the strongest match.
- **DMG MORI NLX 2500 Gen 2 — multi-layer hardware approach.** Spindle spiral oil jacket, coolant circulation through castings, core-cooled ball screws, plus Magnescale direct linear scales. Published: **radial displacement within 7 µm during continuous operation**; 2.0 µm at 3,200 rpm under constant ambient ([Tuyap NLX brochure](https://docs.tuyap.online/FDOCS/95474.pdf); [Gen 2 launch](https://www.marketscreener.com/news/dmg-mori-launch-of-the-nlx-2500-1250-2nd-generation-br-realize-mx-with-process-integration-aut-ce7d58dfd880f72c)).
- **Mazak Integrex i-400S — Ai Thermal Shield.** Chiller-circulated oil around spindle bearings/headstock, ball-screw core cooling, and a **machine-learning compensation model** driven by spindle speed, temperature, position, and coolant state that improves from subsequent measurements ([Mazak accuracy/INTEGREX i NEO](https://www.mazak.com/us-en/products/integrex-i-neo/)). Adaptive rather than deterministic — no published µ-level figure for the i-400S — and learning-cycle dependent; control version on any quoted machine must be confirmed.

**Verdict:** all three can hold ±12.7 µm per part **only if** shop ambient is held near ±1 °C (or compensation is tuned to actual swings), warm-up discipline is observed, and compensation is enabled and verified. Okuma has the strongest published, environment-tolerant data; DMG MORI the best continuous-operation quantification; Mazak the most adaptive but least deterministic approach.

---

## 5. Siemens NX CAM Integration

All three are supported via Siemens NX CAM **Post Hub / Smart Machine Kit Solutions (SMKS, 170+ kits)** ([Siemens Post Hub 2024](https://community.sw.siemens.com/s/article/What-s-new-in-Post-Hub-2024)), but depth differs:

- **DMG MORI — decisive leader.** Manufacturer-certified **MTSK (Machine Tool Support Kit)**: NX postprocessor + machine kinematics model + CSE simulation driver, co-developed by DMG MORI Digital, including simulation of **DMG MORI technology cycles inside NX** — described as unique worldwide — with a dedicated NX support team. Available with SINUMERIK or FANUC controls ([Siemens DMG MORI postprocessor](https://www.siemens.com/en-us/products/dmg-mori-postprocessor-for-siemens-nx/); [DMG MORI Siemens NX](https://us.dmgmori.com/products/digitization/work-preparation/cam-software/siemens-nx)).
- **Mazak — supported, dual path.** Post Hub SMKS kits cover the Integrex family; alternatively Mazak pushes its own MAZATROL Smooth CAM Ai with digital twin. NX is the right choice if your shop standardizes on it, but the integration is not vendor-co-developed to DMG MORI's depth.
- **Okuma — supported, open path.** Post Hub postprocessors plus Okuma's own free adapters on the OSP App Store; the Windows-based OSP-P500 runs third-party posts natively, and THINC API enables custom integration.

**For an NX-standardized aerospace shop, DMG MORI's MTSK pipeline is a material operational advantage** (faster prove-out, verified simulation of actual control behavior); Mazak and Okuma are workable via Post Hub with third-party or community posts.

---

## 6. AS9100D Traceability via MTConnect / OPC-UA

All three meet the data requirements for AS9100D §7.5.3 (records) and §8.5.2 (identification & traceability); differentiators are openness, cybersecurity, and out-of-box completeness:

- **DMG MORI — most open and standards-aligned.** IoT Connector **standard on every new machine since 2020**, simultaneously serving **OPC-UA, MTConnect, and MQTT**; active in the umati companion specification. **CELOS X Tool Master / Tool Data Exchange transfers per-tool, per-cutting-edge identity over OPC-UA** — a digital chain-of-custody that maps directly onto AS9100D tool genealogy requirements ([DMG MORI Connectivity](https://en.dmgmori.com/products/digitization/connectivity); [Tool Master](https://en.dmgmori.com/products/digitization/celos-x/celos-x-tool-master)).
- **Mazak — strongest cybersecurity posture.** All machines MTConnect-capable; **SmartBox 2.0 (Sep 2024)** adds MQTT and OPC-UA on an industrial edge-compute platform with encrypted ports and network segmentation — relevant to records-integrity expectations ([Mazak SmartBox 2.0](https://www.mazak.com/us-en/news-media/news/mazak-advances-machine-connectivity-smart-box-2/)).
- **Okuma — most turnkey genealogy.** MTConnect agent free via the OSP App Store; **OPC-UA server is factory-installed only on specific control variants (OSP-P500M / P700A) — confirm as a line item**, otherwise third-party middleware is required. **Connect Plan Machining Record Management** ties workpiece ID → machining results → gauging results ("who, when, where, what, and the gauging results") with automatic archival — the most out-of-box part-genealogy solution, explicitly aimed at aerospace traceability ([Okuma Connect Plan](https://www.okuma.com/connect-plan)).

---

## 7. Nuevo León Service Infrastructure — Effectively Non-Differentiating

All three OEMs sit **within ~25 km of each other in the Apodaca / San Nicolás de los Garza aerospace corridor** — a geographic redundancy no other Mexican industrial region offers:

| OEM | Facility | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **DMG MORI México** | Citio Torre Aeropuerto, Av. Miguel Alemán 248, Apodaca, N.L. ([locations](https://mx.dmgmori.com/empresa/ubicaciones/dmg-mori-mexico)) | National parts warehouse in Querétaro (expanded 13× to 490 m²); Aerospace Center of Excellence; 01-800-DMG-MORI; NETservice remote diagnostics |
| **Mazak Mexico** | Spectrum 100, Parque Industrial FINSA, Apodaca, N.L. ([Mexico Technology Center](https://www.mazak.com/us-en/about-us/support-bases0/Mexico_Technology_Center/)) | One of 8 North American Technology Centers; named regional service management; 24/7 US hotline 1-800-231-1456; **3 years free MAZATROL training** |
| **Okuma (HEMAQ)** | J. Cantú García 601, San Nicolás de los Garza, N.L.; 25,000 ft² tech center ([Okuma Monterrey](https://www.okuma.com/okuma-tech-centers/monterrey)) | Exclusive distributor since 1989, **4,000+ machines installed**; **CentroTec Monterrey holds AS9100 Rev. D certification** ([HEMAQ](https://www.hemaq.com/venta-maquinas-herramienta-cnc/)) — your QMS can reference their certified processes as audit evidence; 24/7/365 support |

Slight edges: Mazak and DMG MORI are closest to the airport cluster; Okuma/HEMAQ has the deepest installed base and the only explicit AS9100D-certified service operation — meaningful for an AS9100D shop.

---

## 8. Long-Term Operating Cost Drivers

In rough cost-weight order for Ti-6Al-4V aerospace production:

1. **Tooling consumption (largest variable cost).** Carbide insert life in Ti roughing is measured in minutes; consumption is driven by machine rigidity (chatter), HPC effectiveness, and thermal stability. This is where the rigidity/HPC analysis above converts directly to cash. Optimized coolant management alone has documented savings on the order of **~$22,000/yr per machine** (Quaker Houghton case data).
2. **Scrap from thermal drift.** Each scrapped Ti-6Al-4V billet represents **$200–$2,000+ in material** before machining value-add. Published µ-level compensation data (Okuma TFC; DMG MORI Gen 2) reduces dimensional-check frequency, warm-up downtime, and scrap risk; Mazak's learning-based shield requires disciplined tuning to reach the same confidence.
3. **Spindle replacement (~1× per 4–7 years at high duty).** Under a 4,000–6,000 hr/yr regime this is a when-not-if cost. **DMG MORI's 36-month unlimited-spindle-hours warranty is unique here** and directly de-risks the ramp-up years; Okuma's single-source manufacturing (its own spindles, motors, encoders, CNC) minimizes 10–15-year obsolescence and parts-availability risk; Mazak's mature Integrex platform has deep spares logistics, but **the i-400S's possible discontinued status raises long-horizon parts/control-upgrade risk — get a written support-lifecycle commitment.**
4. **Coolant and energy.** DMG MORI claims ~16% energy reduction via GREENMODE plus zero-sludgeCOOLANT options; Okuma's ECO suite (Idling Stop, Power Monitor) automates auxiliary shutdown; Mazak SmartBox analytics support coolant-life monitoring.
5. **Connectivity/data infrastructure.** DMG MORI includes OPC-UA/MTConnect/MQTT standard; Okuma's MTConnect adapter is free but OPC-UA depends on control variant; Mazak SmartBox 2.0 is an accessory line item. Data-driven process optimization is credibly associated with **20–30% cost reductions** in comparable shops.
6. **Hidden/secondary lines to budget:** HPC installation ($30–60k/machine); foundation and floor loading (the i-400S at 16.2 t vs. the NLX at 6.4 t is a real civil-works delta); titanium chip management (hot, stringy, reactive chips — conveyor/scraper design and fire mitigation are safety and AS9100D-relevant); operator training path (MAZATROL conversational vs. CELOS vs. OSP — Mazak's 3-year free training partially offsets ramp-up); CAM post licensing (DMG MORI MTSK vs. Post Hub posts).
7. **Automation retrofit.** All three offer tending/pallet options (DMG MORI Robo2Go, Mazak PLUG-IN Pallet Cell, Okuma cell options) — relevant if the fleet interpretation of the 15,000-hour figure drives toward lights-out operation.

**CAPEX was not quantified by any source reviewed** — obtain formal quotations; expect the Integrex-class platform to carry the highest capital cost, with NLX and Multus in the mid-to-high range.

---

## 9. Composite Decision Matrix

| Factor | DMG MORI NLX 2500SY (Gen 2) | Mazak Integrex i-400S | Okuma Multus U4000 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Heavy Ti shaft turning | ★★★★★ (1,273 Nm opt.) | ★★★★★ (1,400 Nm peak) | ★★★★☆ (955 Nm opt.) |
| Complex 5-axis prismatic Ti | ★★★☆☆ (mill-turn, BMT) | ★★★★★ | ★★★★★ (B-axis + 300 mm Y) |
| ±0.0005" capability | ★★★★☆ (7 µm continuous, documented) | ★★★★☆ (adaptive, unpublished) | ★★★★★ (7–9 µm over 8 °C, JSME-validated) |
| Siemens NX integration | ★★★★★ (MTSK co-developed) | ★★★★☆ (Post Hub) | ★★★★☆ (Post Hub + THINC) |
| AS9100D traceability | ★★★★★ (OPC-UA/MTC/MQTT std; tool genealogy) | ★★★★☆ (SmartBox 2.0, best cybersecurity) | ★★★★☆ (Connect Plan, most turnkey) |
| Nuevo León service | ★★★★☆ | ★★★★★ (Tech Center + free training) | ★★★★★ (AS9100D-certified, 4,000+ installs) |
| Spindle warranty / lifecycle risk | ★★★★★ (36 mo, unlimited hr) | ★★★☆☆ (**verify production status**) | ★★★★☆ (single-source longevity) |

---

## 10. Open Items to Resolve in Writing Before Purchase

1. **Restate utilization as machine-hours/yr per machine** (target 4,000–6,000) and confirm fleet count and shift model.
2. **Mazak:** confirm whether the i-400S is a current build or whether the quotation defaults to the Integrex i NEO successor; confirm which spindle package (1,400 Nm @ 25% ED vs. 500 Nm @ 40% ED) and sub-spindle torque (sources conflict at ~500 vs. ~800 Nm); obtain a written parts/control support-lifecycle commitment.
3. **DMG MORI:** confirm generation (Gen 1 vs. Gen 2 torque figures differ sharply — 426 Nm vs. 843/1,273 Nm) and whether the 12" spindle, Magnescale full-loop feedback, and HPC package are line items.
4. **Okuma:** confirm the high-torque/big-bore spindle (955 Nm), OPC-UA server inclusion on the specific OSP control variant, and HPC option.
5. **All three:** installed HPC cost and performance guarantee; thermal-accuracy acceptance test protocol against ±12.7 µm under your actual shop ambient profile; MTConnect/OPC-UA data-item list mapped to your AS9100D traceability matrix; foundation/power/chiller requirements; training and service-response SLAs for the Apodaca/Monterrey corridor.

**Bottom line:** for a titanium-shaft-dominant, NX-standardized shop, buy the DMG MORI NLX 2500SY Gen 2; for heavy prismatic structural parts, the Mazak (subject to production-status verification); for mixed work under uncontrolled ambient conditions with the strongest local AS9100D-aligned support, the Okuma Multus U4000 with the high-torque spindle — and under a properly restated 15,000-hour fleet plan, standardize on whichever single platform matches your dominant part family rather than mixing fleets.
