final.content:
# WISC-V versus NEPSY-II for the Assessment of ADHD in Children Aged 8–12: A Systematic Literature Review of Working-Memory Sensitivity and Ecological Validity

---

## 1. Executive Summary and Direct Answer

The question "which test has better sensitivity for working memory deficits" admits three different answers depending on which psychometric meaning of *sensitivity* is intended, and a rigorous manuscript must disambiguate them explicitly, because the answers diverge:

| Sense of "sensitivity" | Definition | Answer |
|---|---|---|
| **(a) Statistical sensitivity** (group discrimination; effect size) | Magnitude of ADHD–control differences on a WM measure | **WISC-V WMI wins.** It is a normed, factor-analytically derived composite with replicated medium-to-large group effects (*d* ≈ 0.50–1.18 across studies). The NEPSY-II has no working-memory composite at all and cannot compete on this metric. |
| **(b) Diagnostic sensitivity** (classification accuracy; sensitivity/specificity, AUC) | Ability to correctly identify individual ADHD cases | **Neither instrument is adequate.** WISC-V WMI-based classification yields AUCs of .46–.64 and cross-validated accuracy near chance (~32%); NEPSY-II diagnostic accuracy for ADHD has never been formally established. This is the consensus of the clinical-utility literature. |
| **(c) Incremental validity** (added predictive value beyond other measures) | Whether the measure improves ADHD prediction beyond cognitive testing alone | **The only head-to-head evidence favors the NEPSY-II.** In the single direct comparison (Newberry, 2025; *N* = 272, ages 8–16), NEPSY-II Animal Sorting and Response Set — but not the WISC-V WMI in isolation — independently predicted ADHD diagnosis. This evidence is hypothesis-generating, not confirmatory (see §7). |

**On ecological validity (EV):** No published study has ever compared the ecological validity of the NEPSY-II and the WISC(-V) head-to-head in a pediatric ADHD sample — this absence is itself a reportable finding and a research gap. By task-design analysis (the *verisimilitude* sense of EV), the NEPSY-II's Attention/Executive subtests (Inhibition, Auditory Attention and Response Set, Animal Sorting) place demands on set-shifting, distractor resistance, and rule maintenance that more closely resemble classroom demands than the WISC-V WMI's digit- and picture-span tasks. However, in the *veridicality* sense (empirical prediction of real-world functioning), neither instrument has adequate pediatric ADHD evidence, and both share the fundamental limitation of all performance-based measures: administration in a structured, one-to-one, examiner-scaffolded environment. Performance-based EF measures correlate with rating-based measures at a median *r* = .19 (only 24% of 286 relevant correlations significant; Toplak, West, & Stanovich, 2013), and rating scales (BRIEF-2, Conners 3) outperform both instruments as predictors of real-world ADHD functioning.

**Bottom-line clinical recommendation:** The evidence supports complementary use, not either/or selection — WISC-V as the cognitive-ability frame and exclusionary tool (intellectual disability, learning disorders), NEPSY-II Attention/Executive Functioning subtests as the executive-function screen, supplemented by a continuous performance test (CPT-3/CATA) and multi-informant rating scales, consistent with current multi-method, multi-informant best practice.

---

## 2. Search Strategy

Evidence was assembled through systematic queries of PubMed/PMC, PsycINFO-indexed outlets, Google Scholar, ScienceDirect, SpringerLink, MDPI, Hogrefe, Wiley, and journal-specific repositories, supplemented by backward and forward citation chaining from seminal works. Search strings combined instrument terms ("WISC-V," "WISC-IV," "NEPSY," "NEPSY-II") with diagnostic terms ("ADHD," "attention-deficit," "diagnostic validity," "sensitivity," "specificity," "incremental validity"), construct terms ("working memory," "executive function," "Cognitive Proficiency Index," "central executive"), and methodological terms ("ecological validity," "measurement invariance," "meta-analysis," "factor analysis"). Priority was given to: (i) seminal theoretical and meta-analytic papers (Barkley, 1997; Martinussen et al., 2005; Willcutt et al., 2005; Kasper et al., 2012); (ii) the only direct head-to-head WISC-V/NEPSY-II comparison (Newberry, 2025); and (iii) recent psychometric and diagnostic-utility studies (2018–2026).

**Transparency caveat for peer review:** several paywalled primary sources could be verified only at the abstract level, and a small number of secondary citations (e.g., some non-English-language profile studies) should be re-verified against full text before final citation in the manuscript. These are flagged where they carry inferential weight.

---

## 3. Theoretical Frameworks

Four frameworks structure this literature; identifying which a study adopts is essential because it determines the criterion variable (DSM diagnosis vs. continuous symptom dimensions vs. functional outcome) and the measurement model.

**3.1 Barkley's behavioral-inhibition / executive-function model.** Barkley (1997, *Psychological Bulletin*, 121, 65–94; >5,000 citations) posits that deficient response inhibition produces secondary impairments in four executive functions, of which working memory is paramount; impaired WM returns behavioral control to the "temporal now," generating inattention and impulsivity. Barkley's later work sharpens the ecological-validity critique: EF tests "have very low or no ecological validity" because they sample optimal, examiner-scaffolded performance, and the EF construct itself suffers from definitional proliferation (>20 definitions; up to 33 attributed components) and single-factor solutions in factor-analytic studies of EF batteries ([Barkley, 1997](https://dconducta.es/assets/barkley1997.pdf); [BDEFS excerpt, Guilford](https://www.guilford.com/excerpts/barkley20.pdf); [Barkley self-regulation framework](https://www.vapsych.org/assets/docs/Theory%20of%20Executive%20Function%20%20Self%20Regulation%20-%20Barkley.pdf)).

**3.2 Rapport's working-memory model.** Rapport, Chung, Shore, and Isaacs (2001) reverse the causal priority: WM deficits are hypothesized as central, with disinhibition and hyperactivity downstream. Empirical tests found WM mediated (but did not moderate) the relation between disinhibition and teacher-rated attention problems ([*Journal of Attention Disorders*](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/082957350401900109)). Direct experimental support comes from Kofler et al. (2019): increasing WM load significantly slowed processing speed in children with ADHD (BF₁₀ = 5.82 × 10⁹⁶), whereas reducing processing-speed demands did not impair WM (BF₀₁ = 1.31) — evidence that WM dysfunction is *upstream* of, not secondary to, processing-speed deficits. A 2024 experimental study similarly found that occupying WM capacity slowed RTs and reduced inhibition accuracy in ADHD versus anxious children (*d* = 0.50–1.53), providing "strong evidence against" the claim that WM deficits are merely downstream of inhibition deficits ([*Frontiers in Psychiatry*, 2024](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychiatry/articles/10.3389/fpsyt.2024.1277583/full)).

**3.3 Baddeley's multicomponent model.** The phonological loop, visuospatial sketchpad, and central executive provide the operative measurement taxonomy for the entire meta-analytic literature (verbal/spatial × storage/central-executive). This taxonomy is directly instrument-relevant, because the WISC-V WMI is dominated by auditory-verbal span tasks while the largest ADHD effects are spatial and central-executive (§4).

**3.4 Luria's functional-systems theory (NEPSY-II).** The NEPSY-II is explicitly Lurian: cognition comprises interconnected functional systems, so assessment must separately evaluate each component process; consequently the test derives **no domain composite scores**, and its authors argue that factor analysis is *incompatible* with the instrument's theoretical basis ([Pearson, NEPSY-II Design and Purpose](https://www.pearsonassessments.com/content/dam/school/global/clinical/us/assets/nepsy-ii/nepsy-ii-design-and-purpose.pdf); [*Journal of Pediatric Neuropsychology*, 2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40817-024-00158-8)). **This creates a philosophical asymmetry that any comparative manuscript must acknowledge: the two instruments are not evaluated against the same evidentiary standard.** The WISC-V is judged by factor-analytic and classification metrics its publishers accept; the NEPSY-II's designers pre-emptively reject those metrics.

A supplementary framework, the cognitive-energetic model (Sonuga-Barke, 2003), nests executive and inhibition deficits within state-regulation (activation/effort/arousal) disruption — relevant because it predicts that brief, optimal-condition testing will *underdetect* deficits that emerge under real-world energetic demands.

---

## 4. The Reference Standard: Meta-Analytic Evidence on Working Memory in ADHD

Both instruments must be judged against the established effect-size benchmark for WM deficits in ADHD.

**Martinussen, Hayden, Hogg-Johnson, & Tannock (2005), *JAACAP* 44(4), 377–384** — the field-defining WM meta-analysis (26 studies, 1997–2003). Deficits were independent of comorbid learning disorders and general intellectual ability:

| WM component | Effect size (*d*) | 95% CI |
|---|---|---|
| Spatial storage | 0.85 | 0.62–1.08 |
| Spatial central executive | 1.06 | 0.72–1.39 |
| Verbal storage | 0.47 | 0.36–0.59 |
| Verbal central executive | 0.43 | 0.24–0.62 |

Sources: [PubMed 15782085](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15782085/); [JAACAP abstract](https://www.jaacap.org/article/S0890-8567(09)61489-1/abstract). **This is the single most consequential table for instrument selection:** the WISC-V WMI's core tasks (Digit Span, Letter-Number Sequencing) map onto the *verbal* components — the two *smallest* effects in the field — while the largest effects (spatial storage and spatial central executive) are sampled only partially by the WISC-V (Picture Span, supplementary) and barely at all by the NEPSY-II Attention/Executive domain.

**Willcutt, Doyle, Nigg, Faraone, & Pennington (2005), *Biological Psychiatry* 57(11), 1336–1346** — 83 studies; ADHD *N* = 3,734, controls *N* = 2,969. Medium effect sizes (.46–.69) across EF tasks, strongest for response inhibition, vigilance, working memory, and planning; not explained by intelligence, achievement, or other symptom domains. Critical interpretive anchor: "EF weaknesses are neither necessary nor sufficient to cause all cases of ADHD" ([abstract](https://www.biologicalpsychiatryjournal.com/article/S0006-3223(05)00171-X/abstract)).

**Kasper, Alderson, & Hudec (2012), *Clinical Psychology Review* 32(7), 605–617** — confirmed large between-group effects across both WM domains and identified significant moderators: percent female, number of experimental trials, **recall-versus-recognition format**, and central-executive demands. The recall-format moderator is directly instrument-relevant: WISC-V Digit Span is a recall task, and recall tasks yield different (typically larger) ADHD effects than recognition paradigms ([ScienceDirect](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0272735812000979)).

**Fried et al. (2024), *European Child & Adolescent Psychiatry*** — the largest verbal-WM meta-analysis: 49 studies, *n* = 4,956 ADHD vs. *n* = 3,249 controls on Digit Span Backward; Hedges' *g* = 0.56 (95% CI [0.49, 0.64]), with effect size **decreasing by 0.05 per year of age** — WM deficits attenuate with development, a key consideration for age-restricted inference in the 8–12 band ([abstract](https://www.ingentaconnect.com/content/routledg/clin/2020/00000034/00000005/art00002)).

**Kofler et al. (2020), *Journal of the International Neuropsychological Society*** — bifactor-(s–1) modeling in 172 children ages 8–13. When task unreliability is properly modeled, **central-executive WM impairment is very large (*d* = 1.63–2.03; 75–81% of ADHD children impaired)**, visuospatial short-term storage is moderately impaired (*d* = 0.60; 38% impaired), and phonological short-term storage shows **no deficit**. This reframing is pivotal for the manuscript: the modest classification accuracy of span-based WM measures is partly a *measurement artifact* (unreliability, scoring conventions), not evidence that WM is weakly related to ADHD. Consistent with this, the "Good Holders, Bad Shufflers" analysis shows children with ADHD (especially Inattentive presentation) are differentially worse on backward/manipulation than forward/maintenance spans and on visual-spatial than auditory-verbal spans ([Cambridge/JINS](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/journal-of-the-international-neuropsychological-society/article/abs/good-holders-bad-shufflers)).

**Pievsky & McGrath (2018), *Clinical Psychology Review*** — umbrella review of 37 meta-analyses ranking WM as the **second-largest ADHD-related neurocognitive deficit after reaction-time variability** (weighted mean SMD ≈ 0.54).

---

## 5. Instrument Architecture: Why the Comparison Is Asymmetric

### 5.1 WISC-V

Five primary indexes (VCI, VSI, FRI, WMI, PSI), with ancillary indexes including the Auditory Working Memory Index (AWMI), Cognitive Proficiency Index (CPI = WMI + PSI), GAI, NVI, QRI, NSI, STI, and SRI ([Pearson WISC-V FAQ](https://www.pearsonclinical.ca/content/dam/school/global/clinical/ca/assets/wisc-v-cdn/wisc-v-cdn-faqs.pdf); [*Journal of Psychoeducational Assessment*, 2019](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/0734282919864227)). The WMI comprises Digit Span and Picture Span (Picture Span supplementary); AWMI adds Arithmetic.

Structural validity is strong: in a clinical sample of *N* = 5,359 (47.6% ADHD), a five-factor oblique model fit best, with full metric invariance across diagnostic groups and full scalar invariance across sex and diagnostic groups ([Dombrowski, Watkins, McGill, Canivez, et al., 2021](https://www.ux1.eiu.edu/~glcanivez/Adobe%20pdf/Publications-Papers/Dombrowski,%20Watkins,%20McGill,%20Canivez,%20et%20al.%20(2021)%20WISC-V%20Clinical%20Invariance.pdf)). However, the factor structure is contested: some analyses favor a four-factor higher-order solution over the publisher's five-factor hierarchical model ([*BMC Psychology*, 2026](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40359-026-05191-0)).

### 5.2 NEPSY-II

Thirty-two subtests plus four delayed tasks across six theoretically (not statistically) derived domains; ages 3–16. The Attention/Executive Functioning domain comprises **Animal Sorting, Auditory Attention, Response Set, Clocks, Design Fluency, Inhibition, and Statue**. The manual states explicitly: "Domain scores are not derived in the NEPSY-II due to these psychometric issues and the clinical sensitivity and utility of the individual subtest scores," and "subtests within a domain may not correlate highly with one another" ([Pearson NEPSY-II Chapter 2](https://www.pearsonassessments.com/content/dam/school/global/clinical/us/assets/nepsy-ii/nepsy-ii-design-and-purpose.pdf)).

Two architectural facts are decisive:

1. **The NEPSY-II cannot produce a working-memory index.** Any claim about "NEPSY-II WM sensitivity" is a claim about isolated subtests (e.g., Word List Interference, Memory for Designs, Sentence Repetition) or about WM demands embedded in EF subtests — not about a validated composite. Comparing "WISC-V WMI vs. NEPSY-II WM" therefore requires the analyst to construct an ad hoc NEPSY-II composite, which the manual warns against.
2. **The 2007 revision removed the Tower subtest** (along with Knock and Tap and Visual Attention) and added Animal Sorting, Clocks, and Inhibition ([revision summary, Texas Woman's University](https://twu-ir.tdl.org/server/api/core/bitstreams/cd5d9abc-ac46-4a2a-b0e9-e0689da46eb1/content)). Tower was the battery's dedicated planning measure — and planning is among the strongest ADHD-related EF effects in Willcutt et al. (2005). This is a specific, arguable *capacity reduction* of the NEPSY-II for ADHD-relevant EF coverage that the published comparisons overlook.

**Structural validity concerns.** Independent factor analyses consistently fail to recover the six-domain structure. Brooks et al. (2024, *Child Neuropsychology*), analyzing the norming sample (*N* = 600, ages 7–12), found a best-fitting model with a general factor plus four first-order factors; general loadings were < .50 for most subtests (range .21–.69, *M* = .44), with large subtest-specific variance of unclear construct meaning — supporting the manual's subtest-level interpretive stance but raising the question of *what the subtests actually measure* ([link](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40817-024-00158-8)). A 2024 exploratory analysis of the 7–12 band found a six-factor solution approximating the conceptual domains, but the Social Perception latent dimension could not be reliably located. Stinnett et al. (2002, *Journal of Psychoeducational Assessment*) found a one-factor solution best described the original NEPSY, warning that subtests "should not be interpreted as if they reflect unique neuropsychological processing skills." Finnish norming data yielded four-factor structures diverging from the six domains. Independent reviews by pediatric neuropsychologists (Matthews & Davis, 2010, *Child Neuropsychology*; Davis & Matthews, 2010, *Journal of Psychoeducational Assessment*, ~74 citations) characterize the NEPSY-II as comprehensive and developmentally sensitive but caution against subtest-level over-interpretation and flag standardization-sample concerns ([review](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/09297040903146966); [review](https://exa.ai/library/publication/1fs8mqkt0rv)).

---

## 6. The WISC-V in ADHD: Group Sensitivity Without Diagnostic Accuracy

### 6.1 Group-level working-memory effects (sense (a) sensitivity)

Children with ADHD reliably score lower on WMI and PSI than on other indexes:

- **Martin et al. (2023), *L'Année Psychologique*** — the study closest to the requested age band: 30 ADHD vs. 29 controls, ages 8–12; WMI *t*(57) = 4.52, *p* < .001, ***d* = 1.18**; PSI *d* = 1.13; CPI *d* = 1.14.
- **Tallberg et al. (2018/2021), *Kindheit und Entwicklung* 27(3)** — *n* = 103 German children with ADHD; largest effects on WMI, FRI, and FSIQ; characterized the WISC-V as a "valid and sensitive instrument" for ADHD-related cognitive deficits ([Hogrefe](https://econtent.hogrefe.com/doi/pdf/10.1026/0942-5403/a000256)).
- **García-Mieres et al. (2026), *Actas Españolas de Psiquiatría*** ([PubMed 42343738](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42343738/)) — *n* = 188, ages 6–16; WMI (*p* < .001), PSI (*p* < .001), CPI (*p* < .001), FSIQ (*p* = .005) all lower in ADHD; logistic regression: WMI (B = −0.067, *p* < .001), PSI (B = −0.043, *p* = .007), CPI (B = −0.091, *p* < .001) predicted membership; ADHD-I showed lower WMI than ADHD-C (*p* = .016).
- **MDPI *Sustainability* (2021)** — *n* = 159, ages 6–16; ADHD+SLD children performed worse than controls and SLD-only on WMI, PSI, FSIQ, AWMI, CPI ([link](https://www.mdpi.com/2071-1050/13/17/9948)).
- **MDPI *Behavioral Sciences* (2025)** — WISC-IV, *n* = 719; indexes classified group membership with Nagelkerke *R*² = 0.44 ([link](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-328X/15/9/1279)).

### 6.2 Diagnostic-classification failure (sense (b) sensitivity)

The same literature converges on the failure of WMI-based individual classification:

- **BMC Psychology (2026), *n* = 241, ages 6–17:** medium-to-large ADHD effects on WMI/PSI, but intra-individual discrepancies "are neither sensitive nor specific enough to serve as diagnostic markers" and "may complement, but not replace, other sources of information" ([link](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40359-026-05191-0)).
- **Cross-validated classification study** ([PubMed 42501447](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42501447/)) — *n* = 133, ages 6–16, ADHD vs. SLD vs. ADHD+SLD vs. controls: leave-one-out multinomial accuracy **.32, barely above chance**; neither GAI–CPI discrepancy nor profile configuration differentiated groups; authors advocate a "shared-vulnerability framework."
- **Devena & Watkins (2012)** — ROC analyses of the GAI–CPI discrepancy: AUC = .64 (hospital ADHD vs. normative), **.46** (hospital ADHD vs. referred non-ADHD), .63 (school ADHD vs. normative), .50 (school ADHD vs. matched) — clinically useless discrimination from the populations that actually matter in differential diagnosis.
- **Iranian diagnostic-validity study (2025), *Int J Psychiatry Behav Sci*** — *n* = 250 ADHD vs. 250 controls, ages 7–9: only Processing Speed subtests exceeded critical thresholds; **WM, VC, VS, and FR subtests failed to distinguish groups** ([PDF](https://brieflands.com/journals/ijpbs/articles/153741.pdf)). A companion study (*n* = 240) found WM-domain and PS subtests of the WISC-V Extended valid, with Symbol Deletion most sensitive — partial and culturally bounded evidence ([link](https://maherpub.com/index.php/jndd/article/view/514)).
- **Population base-rate data** ([PubMed 36780371](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36780371/)) — *n* = 865 population 7–8-year-olds: 22% had WM deficits, but the majority had **no** elevated behavioral-regulation or hyperactivity/inattention problems; only 4% had both. Low WMI is neither necessary nor sufficient for ADHD.
- Umbrella clinical-utility reviews concur: cognitive test batteries show "inadequate sensitivity and specificity in identifying ADHD" ([*The Clinical Neuropsychologist*, 2020](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/13854046.2019.1696409)), and IQ/EF measures show no incremental diagnostic validity across 29 studies ([*Assessment*, 2023](https://sage.cnpereading.com/doi/10.1177/10731911231159933)). A 2024 rapid review concluded "there is little clinical utility to undertake a WISC-V in all ADHD assessment cases" ([*The Clinical Neuropsychologist*](https://doi.org/10.1080/20590776.2024.2412336)).

### 6.3 Two mechanistic explanations for the paradox (both must be cited)

The large group effects but poor individual classification have two documented, complementary causes:

1. **Distribution overlap** — ADHD and non-ADHD score distributions overlap substantially, so even *d* ≈ 0.8 yields mediocre AUCs. This is the standard explanation.
2. **Measurement artifact** — (i) Wells et al. (2017) showed the WISC-IV Digit Span discontinue rule has weak construct validity for WM in 8–13-year-olds (*n* = 45 ADHD, 41 controls); **alternate scoring (counting all digits correct rather than trials correct) raised the correlation with WM reordering from non-significant to *r* = .58** and with achievement to *r* = .49 ([PMC5743590](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5743590/)). Standard administration systematically *under-detects* WM deficits. (ii) Kofler et al. (2020) showed correcting for task unreliability more than doubles the estimated central-executive deficit (*d* ≈ 1.6–2.0). (iii) **Schwarze et al. (2024)** conducted the first WISC-V measurement-invariance analysis across ADHD and control groups: configural and metric invariance held, but **full scalar invariance failed**; partial scalar invariance required freeing intercepts for Digit Span, Coding, Symbol Search, and Picture Span — precisely the subtests composing the WMI and PSI ([PMC10817318](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10817318/)). Observed WMI differences may therefore partly reflect measurement non-equivalence rather than pure latent differences, constraining index interpretation in ADHD samples (see also [PubMed 38248904](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38248904/)).

---

## 7. The Direct Head-to-Head Evidence: Newberry (2025)

**Newberry, K. E. (2025). *Pay Attention! A Comparative Analysis of Psychological Assessments and Neurological Mechanisms for ADHD Within a Pediatric Population* (PsyD dissertation, Antioch University Seattle)** is the only direct WISC-V/NEPSY-II comparison in an ADHD sample ([AURA](https://aura.antioch.edu/etds/1127/); [full text](https://aura.antioch.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=2144&context=etds); [OhioLINK ETD](https://etd.ohiolink.edu/acprod/odb_etd/ws/send_file/send?accession=antioch1744236100254081&disposition=inline)).

- **Design:** archival, cross-sectional; *N* = 272 children aged **8–16**; groups by ADHD presentation (Inattentive, Combined/Hyperactive, no diagnosis); binary and multinomial logistic regressions controlling for gender.
- **Measures:** WISC-V (GAI, CPI, VSI, WMI, PSI); NEPSY-II (Animal Sorting, Auditory Attention, Response Set, Inhibition, Word Generation); Conners CPT-3; CATA.
- **Findings:** (a) **lower CPI** and **lower NEPSY-II Animal Sorting and Response Set scores** significantly predicted any ADHD diagnosis vs. no diagnosis; (b) the **WISC-V WMI in isolation was not a robust predictor**; (c) higher CATA scores predicted *lower* likelihood of Inattentive and Combined/Hyperactive diagnoses (a counterintuitive result warranting scrutiny); (d) the NEPSY-II contributed incremental validity beyond the WISC-V. The author concludes the results "support using NEPSY-II, CATA, and CPT-3 for targeted, efficient ADHD assessments over traditional tools like the WISC-V."

**Critical appraisal for peer-review purposes (mandatory):** (i) this is a PsyD dissertation, **not a peer-reviewed publication**, and is not yet indexed in major bibliographic databases; it must be treated as *hypothesis-generating*, not confirmatory; (ii) the age range (8–16) exceeds the requested 8–12 band, so age-restricted inference requires the subset logic of §10; (iii) the archival cross-sectional design precludes causal inference; (iv) logistic regression coefficients, not sensitivity/specificity/AUC metrics, are reported, preventing direct comparison with the diagnostic-accuracy literature; (v) no independent replication exists. **A manuscript that rests its central comparative claim on this single unpublished source will be vulnerable in review**; it should be cited as preliminary evidence justifying a properly designed replication, which the manuscript can frame as its own contribution or agenda.

**Corroborating but weaker adjacent evidence:** Gallo et al. (2025, *Children* 12(6):798) administered WISC-IV + NEPSY-II to *n* = 48 children aged 8–15 (ADHD vs. anxiety disorder vs. comorbid): **no group differences in attention or working-memory measures emerged; only inhibition performance differentiated groups** (longer inhibition RTs in ADHD), leading the authors to recommend routine NEPSY-II Inhibition use in ADHD–anxiety differential diagnosis ([link](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-9067/12/6/798); [IRIS record](https://iris.uniroma1.it/handle/11573/1741790)). A 2015 canonical-correlation study (Ball State, clinical pediatric sample) found WISC-IV WM and PS composites significantly related to NEPSY-II Inhibition-Naming and Inhibition-Switching, but overall canonical correlations were non-significant in the clinically referred sample ([Cardinal Scholar](https://cardinalscholar.bsu.edu/items/1393f480-5723-49c0-b220-23237bd85e25)).

---

## 8. Sensitivity for Working-Memory Deficits: The Synthesis

| Criterion | WISC-V WMI / AWMI | NEPSY-II (Attention/EF + Memory subtests) |
|---|---|---|
| WM construct coverage | Verbal + visuospatial storage and manipulation (Digit Span, Picture Span; + Arithmetic in AWMI) | No WM composite; WM demands embedded in Auditory Attention/Response Set, Inhibition-Switching, Animal Sorting; Memory for Designs and Word List Interference in Memory domain |
| Alignment with largest ADHD effects (spatial/CE; Martinussen 2005) | Partial (Picture Span supplementary; Digit Span Backward engages CE) | Partial-to-good CE engagement via switching/inhibition; minimal dedicated spatial storage |
| Group effect sizes vs. controls | *d* ≈ 0.50–1.18 (replicated) | Limited data; Gallo 2025 found *no* WM group differences; IRIS 2024 descriptively small |
| Individual diagnostic accuracy | Poor: AUC .46–.64; CV accuracy ≈ .32 | Not established for ADHD; Newberry 2025 shows incremental predictive validity for Animal Sorting/Response Set |
| Measurement invariance in ADHD | Partial scalar only (Schwarze 2024) | Never tested in ADHD |
| Known sensitivity-suppressing artifact | Discontinue rule (Wells 2017); correctable by scoring modification | Subtest-specificity/construct ambiguity (Brooks 2024) |
| Incremental validity beyond WISC-V | — | Demonstrated once (Newberry 2025; unpeer-reviewed) |

**Verdict, stated precisely for the manuscript:**

1. **For detecting WM deficits as a construct (statistical sensitivity), the WISC-V WMI is the better-evidenced instrument**, and within it, backward/manipulation conditions and the AWMI (which adds Arithmetic) should be emphasized, because central-executive engagement is where ADHD effects are largest (*d* = 1.63–2.03 when unreliability is modeled; Kofler et al., 2020). Sensitivity can be materially improved by modified Digit Span scoring (counting all digits correct; Wells et al., 2017).
2. **For individual ADHD diagnosis, neither instrument's WM measurement is sufficiently sensitive or specific, and the manuscript must say so plainly**, citing the near-chance cross-validated accuracy and the population base-rate data.
3. **For incremental prediction of ADHD status, the only direct evidence favors the NEPSY-II** (Animal Sorting, Response Set) — plausibly because these subtests better engage the central-executive, set-shifting, and distractor-resistance demands where ADHD effects are largest, and because the WISC-V WMI is verbally weighted toward the smallest-effect components of Baddeley's model. This mechanistic account (modality mismatch) is the most defensible explanation and should be offered as such, explicitly labeled as inference from one unreplicated study plus the meta-analytic moderator pattern.

---

## 9. Ecological Validity

### 9.1 The construct must be operationalized before the instruments can be compared

The EV literature itself is in disarray. Krasny-Pacini and Chevignard (2024, *Journal of the International Neuropsychological Society*) reviewed 90+ EF studies invoking EV and found **only ~28–31% (28 studies) provided any formal definition**; usage conflates criterion validity, construct validity, face validity, and sensitivity/specificity. They recommend the term be defined in every publication or replaced with concrete terminology ([JINS](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/journal-of-the-international-neuropsychological-society/article/conceptualization-of-the-term-ecological-validity-in-neuropsychological-research-on-executive-function-assessment/01C595F6F8931798F9053A0628260BA0)). The manuscript should adopt the **Pinto, Dores, Peixoto, & Barbosa (2023)** framework (82-study systematized review), which decomposes EV into **representativeness/verisimilitude** (artificial↔natural, simple↔complex task demands) and **generalization/veridicality** (statistical prediction of everyday functioning), with a six-stage EV checklist ([record](https://exa.ai/library/publication/2xb6brjjgpy)). A foundational 2012 review in *Applied Neuropsychology: Child* noted pediatric EV research lags far behind adult work ([link](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/21622965.2012.686330)).

### 9.2 Where each instrument sits

**Verisimilitude (task resemblance to real-world demands): NEPSY-II > WISC-V.** The NEPSY-II's Inhibition subtest (suppress automatic naming under time pressure and set-switching), Auditory Attention/Response Set (sustained vigilance with distractors, then rule-switching), Animal Sorting (self-generated conceptual shifting), and Statue (motor persistence with distractions) embed game-like, multi-step, interference-laden demands with face resemblance to classroom behavior regulation. The WISC-V WMI tasks (digit repetition, picture sequencing) are standardized, brief, single-modality, distraction-free, and examiner-paced — high on artificiality. Expert reviews of the NEPSY-II by pediatric neuropsychologists (Matthews & Davis, 2010; Davis & Matthews, 2010; Brooks, Sherman, & Strauss, *Essentials of NEPSY-II Assessment*, Wiley) credit its cross-domain, cross-modality design with better supporting treatment planning and functional description, while cautioning about subtest specificity and the Social Perception domain.

**Veridicality (empirical prediction of real-world functioning): no adequate evidence for either instrument in pediatric ADHD.** Both are administered in identical structured 1:1 environments; Simpson et al. (2024) note such settings "do not reflect daily environments… including conflicting attentional demands," so scores may not indicate real-world ability. The decisive empirical finding is **Toplak, West, & Stanovich (2013, *JCPP* 54(2), 131–143)**: across 20 studies, only 68 of 286 (24%) correlations between performance-based EF measures and rating measures were significant; **median *r* = .19 (~4% shared variance)** — performance tests and ratings "assess different underlying mental constructs" (efficiency of cognitive abilities vs. success in goal pursuit) ([PDF](http://www.keithstanovich.com/Site/Research_on_Reasoning_files/ToplakWestStanovich_2013.pdf)). Toplak et al. (2008) further showed parent/teacher ratings significantly predicted ADHD status while performance-based measures accounted for little unique variance. Barkley's program reaches the same conclusion and grounds the recommendation that EF evaluation must include rating scales (BRIEF-2; Conners 3) alongside any performance measure.

### 9.3 Verdict on the review-of-NEPSY-II-vs-WISC ecological-validity question

The requested "reviews from pediatric neuropsychologists regarding the ecological validity of NEPSY-II compared to WISC" **do not exist as a direct literature** — an important, reportable negative finding. What exists: (i) NEPSY-II reviews praising its functional-systems breadth (an indirect verisimilitude argument); (ii) WISC-V ADHD reviews flagging the structured-environment limitation (an indirect veridicality argument); and (iii) the generic performance-vs-rating literature that impugns both instruments equally. The defensible manuscript claim is: **the NEPSY-II is more ecologically valid by design (verisimilitude), but this advantage is asserted on task-analysis grounds and expert judgment, not demonstrated by comparative predictive-validity data; the claim should be framed as a testable hypothesis, ideally via the Pinto et al. (2023) checklist applied prospectively.**

---

## 10. Methodological Rigor of Key Studies

| Study | Design | *N* | Age | Risk of bias | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|

| García-Mieres et al. (2026) | Case-control; logistic regression | 188 | 6–16 | Low | Subtype differentiation (ADHD-I vs. -C WMI) |
| Schwarze et al. (2024) | MGCFA (German WISC-V) | 91 + 91 | School-age | Low | Partial scalar invariance only — key constraint |
| PubMed 42501447 (2024) | Cross-validated classification | 133 | 6–16 | Low | Accuracy .32 ≈ chance |
| MDPI Sustainability (2021) | Case-control | 159 | 6–16 | Moderate: clinical referral; comorbid SLD | Pattern widespread, non-specific |
| Iran IJPBS (2025) | Psychometric (Davis method) | 250 + 250 | 7–9 | **High**: single-site, non-random, cultural generalizability | Only PSI significant |
| Gallo et al. (2025) | Cross-sectional WISC-IV + NEPSY-II | 48 | 8–15 | Moderate: small *n* | Only Inhibition differentiated groups |
| Wells et al. (2017) | Construct validity | 45 ADHD + 41 controls | 8–13 | Low | Discontinue-rule artifact; scoring fix |
| Kofler et al. (2020) | Bifactor-(s–1) latent modeling | 172 | 8–13 | Low | CE *d* = 1.63–2.03; reliability-corrected |
| Martinussen (2005); Willcutt (2005); Kasper (2012); Fried (2024) | Meta-analyses | up to ~8,200 | Child/adolescent | Low | Reference standard; Fried documents age attenuation |
| Toplak et al. (2013) | Systematic review | 20 studies | Pediatric | Low | Median performance–rating *r* = .19 |

# DiamondRock Hospitality (NYSE: DRH): Does the Financing Strategy Balance Rate-Risk Management With Capital-Allocation Flexibility?

**Verdict: Yes.** Between December 2023 and September 2025, DiamondRock executed a deliberate balance-sheet transformation — retiring all $295.8M of property-level mortgage debt, refinancing it with a new $300M senior unsecured term loan, and layering a partial interest-rate swap overlay over its floating-rate exposure — while total interest expense *fell* 4.6% on a nine-month basis, cash interest paid dropped 9.6%, and operations generated ~$114.8M of free cash flow that covered 100% of distributions. The strategy traded mortgage-secured rate certainty for unsecured prepayability and a fully unencumbered asset base, using swaps to mute (not eliminate) floating-rate risk. The residual exposure is real but quantifiable: roughly $875M of unhedged variable-rate notional as of September 30, 2025.

---

## 1. Interest Rate Swap Fair Values: December 31, 2023 → June 30, 2024

DRH's designated cash-flow-hedge portfolio at year-end 2023 comprised four fixed-payer swaps on senior unsecured term loans totaling **$325M notional** with a combined asset fair value of **$4,321K**. By June 30, 2024, the same four swaps were worth **$3,927K** — a **net change of −$394K (−9.1%)** ([DRH Q2 2024 Form 10-Q, Note 5, SEC](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1298946/000129894624000095/drh-20240630.htm)):

| Swap (pay fixed / receive SOFR) | Notional | Maturity | FV Dec 31, 2023 | FV Jun 30, 2024 | Change |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1.63% | $87,500K | Jul 25, 2024 | $1,660K | $216K | −$1,444K |
| 1.63% | $87,500K | Jul 25, 2024 | $1,658K | $216K | −$1,442K |
| 3.36% | $75,000K | Jan 1, 2028 | $554K | $1,958K | +$1,404K |
| 3.50% | $75,000K | Jan 1, 2027 | $449K | $1,537K | +$1,088K |
| **Total** | **$325,000K** | | **$4,321K** | **$3,927K** | **−$394K (−9.1%)** |

The modest headline decline conceals two economically meaningful offsetting forces:

- **Time decay on near-maturity hedges:** The two 1.63% swaps lost a combined **$2,886K** as they converged to their July 25, 2024 maturity (~25 days of remaining tenor) — exactly the behavior a hedger expects as a fixed-rate position rolls to par.
- **Rate-driven gains on long-dated hedges:** The 3.36% and 3.50% swaps gained a combined **$2,492K** because forward SOFR expectations rose during H1 2024; the longer the remaining tenor, the more the below-market fixed pay rate was worth.

Because these are designated cash-flow hedges, the mark-to-market moves run through OCI and reclassify into interest expense over the hedges' lives — meaning the hedge book was oriented toward locking in low fixed rates rather than harvesting mark-to-market gains, the economically correct posture for a variable-rate borrower. Notably, the **$2,033K non-cash swap mark-to-market charge that hit H1 2023 interest expense was entirely absent in H1 2024**, so on a semi-annual basis total interest expense actually declined $291K (−0.9%), from $32,739K to $32,448K ([Q2 2024 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1298946/000129894624000095/drh-20240630.htm)).

---

## 2. Interest Expense Trend #1: Q2 2023 → Q2 2024

Total interest expense rose **+$635K (+4.1%)**, from **$15,567K to $16,202K** ([Q2 2024 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1298946/000129894624000095/drh-20240630.htm)):

| Component | Q2 2023 | Q2 2024 | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mortgage debt interest | $4,111K | $4,009K | −$102K |
| Unsecured term loan interest | $10,608K | $11,368K | +$760K |
| Credit facility interest & unused fees | $317K | $312K | −$5K |
| Amortization of debt issuance costs | $512K | $513K | +$1K |
| Interest rate swap mark-to-market | $19K | $0 | −$19K |
| **Total** | **$15,567K** | **$16,202K** | **+$635K (+4.1%)** |

The entire increase came from unsecured term-loan interest (+$760K) as SOFR reset higher on the floating-rate unsecured stack — the dynamic the FY2023 10-K attributed to rising SOFR plus the runoff of fixed-rate mortgages retired in 2022 ([2023 10-K MD&A](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1298946/000129894624000011/R9.htm)). Mortgage interest was already drifting down (−$102K). Full-year 2024 interest expense rose only ~$0.4M ($65.1M → $65.5M), with the H1 2023 swap MTM swing accounting for more than the entire net change — evidence the hedge program converted floating-rate volatility into a predictable run-rate.

## 3. Interest Expense Trend #2: Q3 2024 → Q3 2025

This is the more demanding test: during 2025 DRH added a brand-new $300M term loan while retiring its remaining mortgages. Total interest expense rose only **+$125K (+0.7%)**, from **$16,986K to $17,111K** ([DRH Q3 2025 Form 10-Q, SEC](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1298946/000129894625000085/drh-20250930.htm)):

| Component | Q3 2024 | Q3 2025 | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Unsecured term loan interest | $12,665K | $14,223K | +$1,558K (+12.3%) |
| Mortgage debt interest | $3,527K | $1,414K | −$2,113K (−59.9%) |
| Credit facility interest & unused fees | $315K | $504K | +$189K |
| Amortization of debt issuance costs | $479K | $494K | +$15K |
| Finance-lease interest | $0 | $476K | +$476K |
| **Total** | **$16,986K** | **$17,111K** | **+$125K (+0.7%)** |

Management's attribution is direct: the increase "was primarily due to the Amended Credit Facility executed in the third quarter of 2025 which increased our unsecured term loans by $300.0 million, offset by our mortgage debt repayments in 2025." The +12.3% rise in term-loan interest from a larger average balance was almost exactly absorbed by the 59.9% collapse in mortgage interest.

On a **nine-month basis the strategy is unambiguous: total interest expense fell −$2,297K (−4.6%)**, from $49,434K (9M 2024) to $47,137K (9M 2025), with mortgage interest down $4,367K (−37.7%) against only a $434K (+1.2%) rise in term-loan interest and a $1,405K new finance-lease line. The cleanest evidence of hedge effectiveness is cash: **cash interest paid fell 9.6%, from $48,646K (9M 2024) to $43,972K (9M 2025)** — despite an unchanged ~$1.10B debt face and a debt mix shifted decisively toward floating-rate instruments ([Q3 2025 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1298946/000129894625000085/drh-20250930.htm)).

---

## 4. Net Financing-Cost Change: Mortgage Debt → Unsecured Term Loans

**The 2025 transition sequence:**
- **May 6, 2025:** Worthington Renaissance Fort Worth mortgage repaid with cash on hand (≈$75.7M, derived as the residual of total repayments less the two disclosed amounts).
- **July 2–3, 2025:** $60M revolver draw repaid the $53.9M Hotel Clio mortgage at maturity; the bridge was repaid **19 days later** on July 22.
- **July 22, 2025:** Amended Credit Facility upsized from $1.2B to **$1.5B** — a $400M revolver (2030), a $500M term loan (2028), a $300M term loan (2029), and the new **$300M term loan (2030)** priced at SOFR + 1.35%–2.25% on a leverage grid.
- **September 5, 2025:** $166.2M Westin Boston Seaport District mortgage repaid from facility proceeds.

**Total mortgage principal retired: $295,808K**, funded ~1:1 by the $300M new term-loan proceeds — no equity dilution. As of September 30, 2025, **mortgage debt outstanding was $0** and total debt stood at $1.10B at a 5.31% weighted-average rate ([Q3 2025 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1298946/000129894625000085/drh-20250930.htm)).

**Net cost math:**
- Incremental term loan: ~$300M at ~5.3% ≈ **~$15.9M annualized interest**.
- Retired mortgages: ~$295.8M at a blended all-in rate proxied by the ~6.8% weighted average disclosed at mid-2024 (fixed coupons in the ~3.7%–4.4% range plus amortization; the precise per-loan rates were not individually disclosed) ≈ **~$15.7M–$20.1M annualized**.
- **Net recurring financing-cost change: roughly cost-neutral to modestly favorable (−$0.2M to −$4M annualized)**, corroborated by two hard data points: (a) 9M interest expense down $2.3M year-over-year, and (b) full-year 2025 cash interest guidance of **$62–63M, a ~$1.0M reduction at the midpoint** once mortgage paydowns annualize ([Q3 2025 earnings release, Form 8-K Ex. 99.1](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1298946/000129894625000083/exhibit9913q2025.htm)).
- **One-time costs of the transformation:** a **$5,850K loss on debt extinguishment** in Q3 2025 plus **$11,574K of debt issuance costs** paid during 9M 2025 — non-recurring, funded out of proceeds, and excluded from Adjusted FFO.

**The swap overlay is the load-bearing element.** DRH layered a new 3.27%/SOFR swap effective October 1, 2024 and an additional $100M swap effective January 2, 2025 on top of the legacy 3.36%/3.50% positions, holding **effective term-loan rates at ~4.86%–5.01%** even as SOFR reset higher. As of December 31, 2024, $225M of $800M of variable-rate debt was hedged (2024 10-K, Item 7A), with coverage extended into 2025. This deliberate *partial* hedge — enough to cap a meaningful slice of floating exposure while preserving upside if SOFR falls — is what allowed DRH to replace fixed-rate, non-prepayable mortgages with floating-rate unsecured debt at roughly flat cash cost. In exchange it gained: zero secured debt, all debt prepayable without penalty, no maturities before January 2028, and a fully undrawn $400M revolver.

---

## 5. Free Cash Flow: Nine Months Ended September 30, 2025

Using the standard lodging-REIT definition (operating cash flow less capital expenditures), from the Q3 2025 10-Q Consolidated Statements of Cash Flows ([SEC](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1298946/000129894625000085/drh-20250930.htm)) and the Q3 2025 earnings release ([Ex. 99.1](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1298946/000129894625000083/exhibit9913q2025.htm)):

| Item | 9M 2025 |
|---|---|
| Net cash provided by operating activities | **$175,730K** |
| Less: capital expenditures | **($60,941K)** |
| **Free cash flow** | **≈ $114,789K (~$114.8M)** |

Context: FCF of ~$114.8M exceeds net income of $75.2M (D&A of $84.4M is the major non-cash add-back), represents roughly **51% conversion of Adjusted EBITDA** ($225.7M), and — because interest paid is already embedded in operating cash flow — is a **post-financing-cost** figure. On ~206.4M combined shares and OP units, this is approximately **$0.56 of FCF per share** for nine months. (Caveat: the $60.9M capex figure is management's stated amount from the earnings release; full-year 2025 capex guidance was $85–90M.)

---

## 6. How Operations and Capital Allocation Funded the Transformation

The 9M 2025 cash-flow waterfall ([Q3 2025 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1298946/000129894625000085/drh-20250930.htm)):

| Flow | Amount |
|---|---|
| Operating cash flow | +$175,730K |
| Capital expenditures | −$60,941K |
| Mortgage principal repayments | −$295,808K |
| New unsecured term-loan proceeds | +$300,000K |
| Revolver bridge (drawn and repaid) | ±$60,000K |
| Common distributions | −$81,868K |
| Preferred distributions | −$7,362K |
| Share repurchases | −$35,519K |
| Debt issuance costs | −$11,574K |
| Westin Washington D.C. City Center sale (net) | +$89,023K |
| **Net change in cash** | **+$66,628K** |

Three analytical points stand out:

**(a) The refinancing was operationally self-funded at the margin.** Operating cash flow of $175.7M covered capex ($60.9M) *and* all common and preferred distributions (~$89.2M combined) with roughly **$25M+ to spare** — before the term-loan draw or the February 2025 Westin D.C. sale ($92.0M gross, $89.0M net) even entered the picture. Cash on hand nonetheless rose from $81.4M (Dec 31, 2024) to **$145.3M (Sept 30, 2025), +79%**, despite retiring $295.8M of debt and repurchasing $35.5M of stock (~4.8M shares at a $7.72 average). The sequencing — refinance, repay mortgages, restore revolver capacity within 19 days on the Hotel Clio bridge, then buy back stock below book value while sustaining the dividend — demonstrates that the capital-allocation priorities were layered *on top of*, not instead of, the balance-sheet transformation.

**(b) The resulting flexibility is quantifiable, not rhetorical.** Post-transformation, DRH reported book leverage of ~24.8% against a 60% covenant cap, fixed-charge coverage of ~3.24x against a 1.50x minimum, $145.3M of unrestricted cash, and $400M of undrawn revolver capacity — with a 36-hotel, 9,595-room portfolio that is **100% unencumbered**. Annualized FCF of ~$153M covers full-year distributions of ~$119M with a $30–35M cushion, roughly matching the pace of opportunistic buybacks.

**(c) The swap strategy and the capital-allocation strategy are complements.** By capping effective term-loan rates near 4.86%–5.01%, the partial hedge stabilized the interest line (a mere +0.7% Q3-over-Q3 change despite $300M of new debt), which is what made the FCF stream predictable enough to simultaneously fund dividends, buybacks, and cash-funded mortgage repayment. DRH's Adjusted FFO definition explicitly excludes swap fair-value adjustments as non-reflective of underlying performance ([Q1 2024 8-K Ex. 99.1](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1298946/000129894624000048/exhibit9911q2024.htm)).

---

## 7. Residual Risks and Overall Assessment

The strategy is effective but is best characterized as **optionality rather than insulation**:

- **Unhedged floating exposure is now the dominant risk.** With essentially all debt variable-rate and only partially swapped, a 100bp SOFR move flows nearly dollar-for-dollar through interest expense on the unhedged notional (~$875M as of Sept 30, 2025) — partially offset on the upside by swap gains, fully exposed on the downside.
- **Mark-to-market reversal.** By September 30, 2025, several of the fixed-payer swaps had swung from small assets to small liabilities — a non-cash, OCI-borne item excluded from Adjusted FFO, but a source of future reported volatility as positions reclassify into earnings.
- **One-time costs were real:** $5.85M extinguishment loss plus $11.6M of issuance costs (~$17.4M combined) is the upfront price of the flexibility gained, and no rigorous counterfactual (what interest expense would have been with *no* swaps in a rising-SOFR environment) is disclosed — though the 9.6% decline in cash interest paid is strong circumstantial evidence of a positive hedge payoff.

**Bottom line:** The numbers converge on an effective strategy. The swap portfolio's fair value moved only −$394K (−9.1%) from December 2023 to June 2024, with healthy internal offset (time decay on expiring 1.63% hedges versus +$2.5M of gains on long-dated 3.36%/3.50% hedges). Interest expense rose just +0.7% from Q3 2024 to Q3 2025 despite $300M of incremental term loans, and *fell* 4.6% on a nine-month basis as mortgage interest collapsed 59.9% in Q3. The mortgage-to-unsecured transition was approximately cash-cost-neutral to modestly accretive (FY2025 cash interest guidance cut ~$1M to $62–63M), and ~$114.8M of nine-month free cash flow — covering 100% of distributions with room for $35.5M of buybacks and a cash-funded mortgage payoff — is what allowed DRH to fund a $295.8M debt refinancing through operational cash generation plus a like-sized term-loan draw, ending September 2025 with zero secured debt, no maturities before January 2028, $145.3M of cash, and a fully undrawn $400M revolver.

**Primary sources:** [DRH Q2 2024 Form 10-Q (SEC)](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1298946/000129894624000095/drh-20240630.htm); [DRH Q3 2025 Form 10-Q (SEC)](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1298946/000129894625000085/drh-20250930.htm); [DRH Q3 2025 earnings release, Form 8-K Ex. 99.1 (SEC)](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1298946/000129894625000083/exhibit9913q2025.htm); [DRH FY2023 Form 10-K MD&A (SEC)](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1298946/000129894624000011/R9.htm); [DRH Q1 2024 earnings release, Form 8-K Ex. 99.1 (SEC)](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1298946/000129894624000048/exhibit9911q2024.htm).
